The team found the hormone lowers levels of Kit, the receptor for stem cell factor. A kinase named Lyn helps carry that effect. The finding shows two growth signals trading places as a cell matures. In leukemia, that trade is jammed, and knowing the wiring may suggest ways to free it.
plos-pone-0005821:
Nikolai Khodarev and co-authors reported in 2009 that a signal pathway tied to interferon can, paradoxically, help tumors spread and resist treatment. STAT1 signaling is classically antiviral and tumor-suppressing. But tumors with the pathway stuck on can behave more aggressively.

The team tested whether STAT1 activity amplifies metastatic potential and therapy resistance. Their results supported that darker role in their models. The same pathway can be friend or foe depending on context, a common theme in cancer. Knowing which tumors run it hot may predict which ones need harder treatment.
plos-pone-0006421:
Karl Friston, Jean Daunizeau, and Stefan Kiebel wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE theory paper on how agents learn to act. They ask whether reinforcement learning, where acts are shaped by rewards, is really needed at all. Control theory comes under the same doubt. Their answer rests on a free-energy view of perception.

The authors show that an agent can learn complex, flexible acts by adjusting its inner states to cut surprise. No reward signal has to drive the process. Perception and action become two sides of one self-tuning system. The argument offers a fresh base for thinking about brains and smart machines.
plos-pone-0006521:
Ioannis Stylianou and co-authors described a mutant mouse with a liver-specific defect in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cardiovascular disease is the largest cause of premature death worldwide. Circulating plasma lipid levels are a key risk factor, and scavenger receptor class B member 1 helps control them. The team used ENU mutagenesis, a chemical method, to create point mutations.

One novel mutation caused loss of the receptor in the liver specifically, as their title reports. A liver-only loss lets researchers separate liver roles from effects elsewhere. Such mice are precision tools for lipid research. They may clarify how this receptor protects against heart disease.
plos-pone-0006621:
Enitan Carrol and co-authors tested blood markers of severe bacterial infection in Malawian children in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fast spotting of these infections, and fast use of the right drugs, can cut child deaths by a large share. The team checked the accuracy of five markers in children thought to have severe infections. They weighed how well each marker finds the disease and how well it predicts the outcome.

In clinics with few tools, a cheap blood marker can guide who needs urgent care most. A marker must do both jobs well to earn its place. Their results help hospitals pick markers that work on the ground there. Tests should be proven where they will be used, not just where they were made.
plos-pone-0009421:
Danielle Doucet and co-authors published this rat trauma study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Severe injury with heavy bleeding often ends in lung damage and organ failure. A key step is gut injury: starved of blood, the gut leaks and inflames. That gut damage then drives harm to the lungs.

The team tested drugs that activate the estrogen receptor in rats after trauma and hemorrhagic shock. The treatment limited injury to both gut and lung. A hormone-based shield against the cascade could help trauma care, where minutes matter and options are few. The study identifies a pathway worth testing for that protection.
plos-pone-0009521:
Craig Atencio and Christoph Schreiner mapped sound circuits in cat cortex in PLOS ONE in 2010. The primary auditory cortex is the first cortex area to handle sound. Its cells are laid out in columns that run through stacked layers. Signals move both up the columns and across the layers. The team recorded cell activity to trace that flow.

Their map shows how the microcircuit extracts features from sound and passes them on. Different layers play distinct roles in the chain. Knowing the routing helps explain how raw sound becomes a signal the brain can use. It grounds models of hearing in direct measures.
plos-pone-0009621:
Thomas Richardson and co-authors looked at records and extremes in ant colonies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ant societies divide work among many members. Some leave the nest to forage or patrol, while others stay home. The team studied the dynamics of individual activity over time. They asked how record breaking bursts of work arise and fade in such a system.

Patterns in those records matched ideas from the study of other complex systems. Simple rules at the level of one ant can yield rich colony behavior. The work links ant labor to a broader science of extremes and records. It helps explain how a colony stays efficient without any central plan.
plos-pone-0010421:
Jérôme Verine and colleagues tested a possible marker for a common kidney cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clear cell renal cancer is the most frequent type of kidney tumor. No specific marker existed to detect or track it. The team had earlier found a gene, angptl4, switched on strongly in these tumors. It responds to low oxygen, a common tumor condition. They asked whether its message RNA could serve as the marker.

A good marker should flag both first tumors and spread ones. It should also appear in samples doctors can actually take. Testing the RNA in patient material was the next step this study took. Kidney cancer found early is far more curable. A reliable marker would change how it is watched and treated.
plos-pone-0010521:
Jan Bressler and colleagues tested whether a fat-linked gene raises diabetes risk differently by ancestry in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the gene FTO track with higher body weight in European groups. One variant also raised diabetes risk when first found in a genome-wide scan. The team used the long-running ARIC study of American adults. They compared effects in white and African-American participants.

The gene's link to weight and diabetes was not the same in both groups. Such differences warn against exporting genetic findings across populations unchecked. They also hint that the gene acts through paths that vary with background and environment. Large mixed cohorts like ARIC are essential for fair genetic medicine. This study uses one to keep conclusions honest.
plos-pone-0010621:
Dorret Boomsma and colleagues estimated how much of adult ADHD is inherited, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most heritability work on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder used children. Far less was known about adults, whose symptoms often persist.

The team scored adults with a standard ADHD index and compared relatives. Genetic factors explained a large share of the differences in scores. Shared childhood surroundings explained much less. The result supports treating adult ADHD as a strongly heritable condition. That shapes how doctors think about family risk, screening, and long-term care for adults.
plos-pone-0010721:
Julia Rausenberger and colleagues built a full model of how a plant light sensor works, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phytochrome B is a protein that reads red light and steers plant growth. A seedling in shade grows tall and pale; in open light it grows short and green. The sensor's protein dynamics drive that whole-body choice.

Their model links the sensor's slow molecular switching to growth outcomes. It predicts how plants react when light flickers or changes color. Few models in plant science span from single proteins to whole seedlings. A working bridge between those scales can guide crop breeding for dense planting, where shade responses cost yield.
plos-pone-0010821:
John Pisciotta, Yongjin Zou, and Ilia Baskakov measured electric current from cyanobacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyanobacteria are ancient microbes that capture sunlight and release oxygen. They account for a large share of Earth's photosynthesis. Whether living cells hand off part of that captured energy as current was an open, testable question.

In light, the bacteria produced a measurable electric current. In darkness the current fell away. The flow thus came from photosynthesis itself, not from stored food. Living solar cells remain far weaker than panels. Still, the proof matters: biology can be wired directly. That is a step toward devices that grow their own power source.
plos-pone-0010921:
Alexei Samsonovich and Giorgio Ascoli published this language study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Computers that map word meanings usually place words in spaces with hundreds of dimensions, each tied to a narrow topic, and they often miss that opposites are closely related. The authors built a simpler kind of semantic map using a self-organizing method.

Their low-dimensional map places synonyms near each other and antonyms in an orderly relation, without being told any meanings in advance. Its first three axes came out cleanly interpretable: good versus bad, calm versus excited, and open versus closed. Samsonovich and Ascoli show that a handful of deep dimensions may underlie how minds organize meaning. A compact meaning map could power better automated text analysis and sharpen theories of how people judge words.
plos-pone-0011021:
Peter Loudon, Eric Yager, Debbie Lynch and co-authors published this flu vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent bird and swine flu outbreaks kept the pandemic threat vivid, and DNA vaccines promise fast manufacture and possibly broader protection. The team tested an H1N1 DNA vaccine shot into the skin of rhesus macaques by a gene gun, with a growth factor added as a booster.

Macaques were immunized three times over sixteen weeks with the vaccine encoding a flu surface protein, with or without GM-CSF, a factor that recruits immune cells. Loudon and colleagues measured responses both in the blood and at mucosal surfaces, where flu first enters. Their work tests whether a skin-delivered DNA vaccine, helped by an immune recruiter, can protect at the respiratory front line as well as systemically, a combination pandemic planning needs.
plos-pone-0011121:
Mancuso, Sammarco and Grabczyk studied a jumping gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The element, called Tn7, can cut itself from one DNA spot and paste into another. The team asked what kinds of DNA spots it prefers when the DNA folds into a triple strand shape.

Tn7 favored repeated three letter DNA runs when those triple strand forms could arise. Knowing a jumping gene's favorite targets helps predict where it will land. That knowledge is useful for genome science and for designing safer gene tools. It also links DNA shape, not just DNA letters, to where genes move.
plos-pone-0011221:
Polato, Voolstra, Schnetzer and colleagues heated young corals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Larvae of a reef building coral came from several locations. The team exposed them to thermal stress and compared how larvae from each place responded at the gene and survival level.

Responses differed by home location, showing local variation in heat tolerance. That variation is a resource for reef recovery: tougher larvae can seed new reefs. As oceans warm, planting heat tolerant corals gives reefs a better chance. The study helps managers choose source sites for restoration with climate in mind.
plos-pone-0011321:
Curlin, Huang, Lu and colleagues tested gut samples from men in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human adenovirus, a common virus family, was sought in gut samples taken from the men in this study. The team measured how often the virus could be detected there.

Detection was frequent, showing the virus persists in the gut more than expected. That persistence matters for HIV vaccine research, since some HIV vaccine approaches use adenovirus as a carrier. Prior gut exposure could change how such vaccines perform in trials. The finding helps trial designers interpret results in this population.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1221:
A second Hurley dispatch to the Secretary of State bears the same date, 29 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the China post signal a file moving too fast for one report. Hurley's embassy dealt with a government, an army, and a rival party all at once.

Back-to-back dispatches let an envoy split subjects: one for the urgent, one for the standing picture. Together they kept Washington's China brief full during the summit's close. This one is the day's companion piece. Read as a pair, the two cables show the tempo of a post where the next war was already taking shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1321:
Parten, chief of staff of the American reparations team, wrote to Pauley, its head, on 21 July 1945. The note ran inside the mission that judged Germany's capacity to pay. Parten ran its staff work; Pauley carried its findings to the summit.

Internal notes of a mission fix facts, assign tasks, and ready the chief's brief. This one dates from the heart of the reparations fight at Potsdam. It shows the mission's machine at work behind its famous head. The figures that leaders quoted in the great rooms began in staff traffic of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1421:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. The date falls just before the conference formally opened, when delegations were tabling their opening positions.

Early texts at a summit stake out ground. A paper tabled before the leaders even sat down shows a delegation arriving with its asks already drafted. Readers can follow this Soviet text forward through the talks: which of its points the final protocol kept, and which the other powers bargained away. The closing run of the volume gathers many such texts, letting the drafting fight be read whole.
frus-1945-50-intel-d21:
General John Magruder, who now ran the Strategic Services Unit in the War Department, wrote to three intelligence chiefs at once on 1 October 1945. His unit was the surviving core of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Magruder's letter went to the Army's intelligence chief, the Navy's, and the State Department's new research and intelligence head. That mailing list is the post-OSS world in miniature: three services and one department, each holding a piece. Readers meet here the man trying to keep the remnant alive while the pieces were argued over. His papers through the autumn form the volume's thread of survival, written from inside a unit that everyone expected to vanish.
frus-1945-50-intel-d121:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946, the same day the National Intelligence Authority wrote to Clark. The FBI director's letter answers the board's move from inside the Justice Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hoover rarely accepted a ruling against the bureau without putting his objection in writing to his own chief. His letter of 8 August belongs to the peak of the Latin American fight, when the board's decision on the field was being delivered. Readers can read the day whole: the authority's letter and Hoover's response, claim and counter-claim, preserved side by side. The volume's fairness in printing both is what makes it history rather than a victor's tale.
frus-1945-50-intel-d221:
Dated 18 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the Intelligence Advisory Board. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 221, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d321:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) addressed a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) on 29 July 1947. The State Department prints it as document 321 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d421:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, Bissell, on 8 May 1950. The memo is document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Within weeks, war in Korea would test every part of the system these men ran. In May the work was still one of charts, duties, and shared reports. The memo shows the CIA chief dealing with Army intelligence at staff level, where the real links were made. Bissell's office linked the Army's field reports to the joint picture the CIA tried to build.
frus-1861-d21:
Henry Sanford, the American minister to Belgium, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1861. The dispatch is document 21 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Brussels sat close to both Paris and London, and Sanford prized news from each. His reports mixed court talk with press and market word. For Washington, such letters were a cheap way to keep eyes on Europe's mood in the war's first spring. Belgium's king, Leopold, had wide family ties in Europe, which made Brussels talk worth hearing. Talk in Brussels often reached Seward before the same news came by formal note.
frus-1861-d121:
Charles Faulkner wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 April 1861. The dispatch is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner stayed at the Paris post until Dayton could arrive. His April report came three days after Fort Sumter, from a capital full of war talk. It shows an outgoing envoy still serving the new chief through the handover. His service bridged two parties and two cabinets in the space of a few weeks. Bridging two cabinets in weeks was a strain few envoys of the age could match.
frus-1861-d221:
By the date of 22 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Marsh. Congress received it as Document 221 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d21:
By the date of 11 February 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 21 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d121:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 7 August 1862. Congress received it as Document 121 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d221:
On 1 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 221 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter opened the month's run of Seward-Stuart exchanges.

July began with McClellan's army pulling back from Richmond, a retreat that looked like defeat abroad. Foreign governments read Union weakness as a reason to push for a truce. Against that mood, Seward kept his tone even and his letters frequent. This one belongs to the effort to steady nerves in the first days of a bad month. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d321:
Two Dayton reports are dated 3 September 1862, and the first stands as Document 321 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote three days after Bull Run, before the defeat's full weight had reached Paris. The French government was then drafting its proposal for a joint truce, the fall's central danger. Reports from these days show the envoy gathering the court's mood while the ground shifted under his information, a fair picture of his craft. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d421:
On 30 May 1862 Horace J. Perry reported from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his last letter home. The report is Document 421 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Frequent short reports kept Washington current in an age when mail moved by steamer. Perry covered the Spanish court's view of the war, its Cuban concerns, and its part in the Mexican affair. In the last days of May 1862, French forces had just been checked at Puebla, news that changed the tone in Madrid. Perry's dispatches let a reader follow that shift as the legation saw it, week by week.
frus-1862-d521:
On 24 September 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 521 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's letter was dated two days after Lincoln issued the preliminary emancipation order, but the news had not yet reached the Netherlands. He wrote instead of the Dutch scene as it stood: cautious, commercial, and waiting on American battle news. The gap between the date on the page and the facts on the ground is the story of all these letters. Seward, reading in October, could correct for it; the modern reader should too, and will find the Hague file a clear window on that lag.
frus-1862-d621:
On 10 January 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman reported from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 621 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Haldeman opened the year reporting Swedish goodwill and the north's reading of the war after the Trent settlement. Sweden and Norway sent the Union settlers and sailors rather than trouble, and their government's neutrality was never in question. Still, Seward wanted every post reporting, and Stockholm's letters fixed the friendly north in his survey of Europe. The report is part of the early-1862 round of the Department's work. In that round it confirmed, capital by capital, where it stood. The crisis with Britain had by then passed.
frus-1863p1-d21:
For the last time in 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 29 December. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 21 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, Seward's last to London in the old year.

Seward wrote days before the freedom edict for the enslaved took force on New Year's Day. That act would change the war's face abroad, and his envoys had to be ready to speak for it. This letter belongs to that hinge in time. It shows Washington briefing its London man at the close of a year that had tested the Union and its foreign ties alike.
frus-1863p1-d121:
Third in its set comes this letter of 16 March 1863 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 121 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By the third sheet, a batch turns from the great heads to the finer ones. Seward's file for Britain held many small claims and talks, each worth its own page. This letter is the third of the 16 March set. It shows the depth of the brief that one envoy carried, and the care with which Washington stocked him for it.
frus-1863p1-d221:
The mail from London dated 25 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 221 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d321:
A formal note dated 13 November 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 321 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d421:
From the British legation in Washington on 23 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada bordered the Union along a long, thinly guarded line. British worries about that frontier, and American worries about plots hatched there, fed part of this mail. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d521:
Under the date 21 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d621:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 22 September 1863 and wrote to William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020021:
Xuan Wang and James E. Haber studied DNA repair in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When both strands of DNA break, the cell can fix the gap by copying from a matching strand. A protein called RPA coats loose single strands of DNA during that repair.

The step in focus is strand invasion, when the broken end pushes into the intact copy to start the fix. The authors test what RPA does at that exact moment. Getting this right matters because failed repair can lead to cancer or cell death. Yeast offers a clean test bed for the basic steps. The same core repair tools work in human cells, so the lessons carry over.
plos-pbio-0020321:
Sean R. Collins, Adam Douglass, Ronald D. Vale, and their team watched prion growth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Prions are protein clumps, called amyloids, that grow as more copies of the protein join and fold the same wrong way. In yeast, this growth can be filmed and measured with care.

The team found the clumps grow by adding one protein unit at a time, not by merging smaller clumps. That single detail shapes every model of how prions spread. It rules out some theories and supports others. Amyloid growth also sits behind diseases like Alzheimer's. So a clean growth rule in yeast has reach far beyond the test tube.
plos-pbio-0020421:
Mathias Currat and Laurent Excoffier modeled ancient human mating in PLOS Biology in 2004. As modern humans spread into Europe, they met Neandertals already living there. Whether the two groups mixed has long been debated from fossils and DNA.

Their model shows that even rare mixing would likely have left clear traces in today's DNA, given how the expansion unfolded. Since such traces were then unseen, they argue the two groups did not admix, or mixed far less than some claimed. Modeling like this sets the bar for what counts as evidence. It turns a debate of impressions into a test with numbers that DNA studies can check.
plos-pone-0000121:
Rony Zachariah, Anthony David Harries, Marcel Manzi, and colleagues published this health study from rural Malawi in PLOS ONE in 2006. It concerns patients infected with both HIV and tuberculosis who were offered anti-retroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check. The team measured how many patients accepted the treatment.

Their finding, stated in the title, is blunt: acceptance was low, and the cost of transport to reach care was a key barrier. The paper shows that free medicine alone does not get people treated when a bus fare stands in the way. It remains a clear case study for programs fighting HIV in poor rural regions.
plos-pone-0000221:
Amane Koizumi, Günther Zeck, Yixin Ben, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes organotypic culture of adult mammalian retinas, keeping the light-sensing tissue of the eye alive and working outside the body. The cultured retinas stay physiologically functional, responding much as they would in a living eye.

A working retina in a dish lets researchers test drugs and study vision diseases without whole animals at every step. The authors show their culture method preserves that function. The system is a platform for studying retinal disease and for screening treatments aimed at saving sight.
plos-pone-0000321:
Marylyn M. Addo, Rika Draenert, Almas Rathod, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fully differentiated CD8 T effector cells are the most battle-ready killer cells against HIV. The authors report these cells are detectable more often in controlled HIV-1 infection than in progressive infection, where the virus wins.

The contrast suggests that having these mature killers on hand goes with keeping the virus in check. The authors compare patients who control the virus with those who do not. The pattern helps define what a protective immune response against HIV actually looks like, a target for vaccine design.
plos-pone-0000421:
Michael P. Cusack and colleagues used network math to find the amino acids a protein can least afford to lose, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method needs only the protein's structure. By treating the structure as a network of contacts, they identified critical residues, the positions where change is most likely to break the protein.

Knowing the critical spots in advance guides experiments: those are the positions worth mutating, and the ones where natural variants may cause disease. A method that works from structure alone can scan proteins that have never been studied in the lab. The paper is an early example of network analysis moving into protein biology.
plos-pone-0000521:
Nils Arrigo and Claire Arnold documented escaped grapevines reshaping European landscapes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Many European vineyards grow on rootstocks bred in North America to resist pests; these naturalised Vitis rootstocks have spread into the wild. The team studied the consequences for the native wild grapevine.

Escaped rootstocks can hybridize with wild relatives, diluting the native gene pool, and can also carry diseases. The wild grapevine is itself a relic subspecies worth protecting. The study shows farm technology leaking into ecology. A solution bred for farms becomes a pressure on the crop's wild ancestor.
plos-pone-0000621:
Andres Baena, Alan R. Mootnick, James V. Falvo and their co-authors compared a key immune gene across primates in PLOS ONE in 2007. TNF, short for tumor necrosis factor, is a signaling protein central to the immune response. The promoter, the DNA stretch that switches the TNF gene on, is strongly conserved in mammals and especially in primates.

Small spelling differences in that promoter, called SNPs, drew the team's attention. Their title reports that these promoter patterns mark primate family relationships and trace how innate immunity evolved. Readers interested in both evolution and immunology get a case where one gene's control region tells both stories at once.
plos-pone-0000721:
Frank A. J. L. Scheer, Kenneth P. Wright, Richard E. Kronauer and colleagues tested how far the human body clock can stretch. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study was motivated by Mars: a Martian day, or sol, lasts 24.65 hours. That lies outside the range the human circadian pacemaker can entrain to under typical astronaut lighting. Failing to entrain would scramble sleep and performance.

The authors examine plasticity in the clock's intrinsic period, asking whether the period itself can adapt. If the pacemaker can lengthen its own cycle, mission planners gain a biological solution to the sol problem. The results also matter for shift workers and jet lag on Earth.
plos-pone-0000821:
Lyse A. Norian and Paul M. Allen found that anti-tumor T cells grow up fast inside tumors, but not elsewhere, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Increasing the efficacy of adoptively transferred, tumor-specific T cells is a major goal of immunotherapy, where patients receive lab-grown immune cells. A fuller grasp of the effector phase of T cell responses would clearly help. It must come from the tumor site itself. Most studies instead sample blood or lymphoid organs.

Their title reports rapid maturation of effector T cells in tumors during tumor regression, absent in lymphoid organs. The battlefield changes soldiers faster than the barracks does. Sampling tumors directly could reveal what successful immunotherapy actually looks like.
plos-pone-0000921:
Francesca Gabanella, Matthew Butchbach, Luciano Saieva and co-authors linked faulty particle assembly to severity in spinal muscular atrophy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The disease weakens motor neurons and is caused by low levels of a protein called SMN. SMN works with partner proteins to assemble small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, machines the cell needs to process its messages.

The team asked whether how badly assembly fails matches how severe the disease is. They also found the defect hits a subset of those particles hardest. A match between a lab defect and real severity supports the idea that failed assembly drives the illness. It also points to where a therapy would need to act.
plos-pone-0001021:
Steven Frank examined the puzzle of robustness in evolution, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Organisms buffer themselves against disturbance in many ways. Repair fixes damage, feedback loops hold body systems at their set points, and chemical filters sort signal from noise.

The puzzle is that strong buffering can also permit maladaptation, hidden flaws that surface later. Frank works through why protection and fragility grow from the same machinery. The paper is theory, aimed at the logic of evolution rather than one species. Its value is a clear frame for cases from drug resistance to genetic disease, where robustness cuts both ways.
plos-pone-0001121:
Jellyfish rarely fossilize well, since their bodies are soft and mostly water. Paulyn Cartwright and co-authors report a striking exception in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe jellyfish fossils preserved in unusual detail in Middle Cambrian rocks, from roughly half a billion years ago.

Cnidarians, the group that includes jellyfish, split off early in animal history, so their fossils bear on how animal life first diversified. The authors describe what these specimens preserve and what they show about early jellyfish. The finds also matter because jellyfish remain a major part of ocean plankton today.
plos-pone-0001221:
Notch signaling, a conversation between neighboring cells, decides the fates of cells throughout development. Bon-Kyoung Koo and colleagues examined a protein called Mind bomb-1 in mammalian development, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Notch signaling requires that ligand molecules on one cell be pulled inside it, a step handled by ubiquitin ligase enzymes.

The authors report an obligatory role for Mind bomb-1 in mammalian Notch signaling: without it, the pathway fails. Two families of these ligases, Neuralized and Mind bomb, were known to cooperate in flies. Showing that one is indispensable in mammals sharpens the picture of a fundamental pathway.
plos-pone-0001321:
Salvianolic acid B is one of the most active components of Salvia miltiorrhiza. That plant is a traditional Chinese herbal medicine used for disorders of the brain's blood vessels. Chen-Li Liu and colleagues studied how it protects blood vessel lining cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Hydrogen peroxide, an oxidant, can push endothelial cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death.

The authors report that salvianolic acid B inhibits that peroxide-induced apoptosis through regulating PI3K/Akt signaling, a major survival pathway in cells. The protective effects of the herb were known in practice, but the mechanism was not. Their work connects a traditional remedy to a defined molecular route.
plos-pone-0001421:
Sarah Chapelsky and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a plant compound that may block anthrax toxin. Anthrax germs owe much of their harm to a toxin that weakens host defense. A known effect is the bursting of immune cells in culture. The team tested whether the compound celastrol could stop that bursting.

In mouse immune cells, the compound did hold back toxin driven cell bursting. That marks it as a lead worth more study, not yet a drug. Leads that shield host cells take a path unlike germ killing drugs. They may keep working even when germs resist standard drugs, which keeps this line of work of interest.
plos-pone-0001521:
Clotilde Randriamampita and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tool to watch T cell signals live. How a T cell tells friend from foe with such speed and care was still debated. Space and time control of signals was thought to be key. The team built a sensor that glows when a core T cell enzyme is active.

With the sensor, they watched the enzyme fire both at the contact point and at the far side of the cell. That far side firing was a surprise. Live sensors like this turn fixed cell views into films. They let labs test signal theories as the acts unfold.
plos-pone-0001621:
Anand Kolatkar, Kevin Kennedy, Dan Halabuk, and their colleagues presented a software tool called C-ME in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. C-ME stands for Collaborative Molecular Modeling Environment. It lets research teams work together in a shared 3D space in real time, even when team members are in different places.

The authors note that big projects spanning many fields now produce data stored in separate places. There is no easy way to view it as a whole. Their tool was built to close that gap for work such as proteome-wide studies, which cover all the proteins in a cell or organism. The full text explains how the tool works, what it can show, and how research and training groups can use it to study molecules together.
plos-pone-0001721:
Ziad Obermeyer, Jesse Abbott-Klafter, and Christopher J. L. Murray assessed the world's main tuberculosis strategy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. DOTS, the WHO strategy built on directly observed treatment, had been running nearly fifteen years, yet tuberculosis stayed a major global health problem. With little hard evidence that DOTS cuts the burden, its future role was under debate.

The authors gathered empirical data on whether DOTS improved case finding or treatment success. The full text gives the countries and data sources, the measures compared, and what improvements, if any, the strategy delivered. An honest audit matters because TB programs worldwide spend heavily on this framework, and policy should follow results, not habit.
plos-pone-0001821:
Ron X. Yu and co-authors presented a method to find direct target genes of transcription factors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A major challenge of the post-genome era is reconstructing regulatory networks from accumulated biological knowledge. Tools for identifying direct targets, genes a factor switches on by binding them, are critical to that effort.

Their approach uses joint sequence and expression likelihood, weighing DNA sequence and activity data together. They applied it to DAF-16, a longevity-linked factor in worms. The full text gives the method and the target lists. Distinguishing direct targets from downstream echoes is what turns a gene list into a wiring diagram.
plos-pone-0001921:
Martin Alphonse and co-authors studied an allergy receptor on a white blood cell type in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The receptor, Fc epsilon RI, binds the antibody IgE and plays a key role in allergic asthma. The team had shown that neutrophils, a front-line immune cell, from people with allergic asthma carry a working form of this receptor.

They then asked what controls how much of the receptor these cells show. Two suspects were in view: contact with allergens across the seasons, and Th-2 signals, the immune messages that drive allergy. Knowing the controls could point to new ways to calm asthma at its source.
plos-pone-0002021:
Pablo Tebas and co-authors studied what happens when HIV treatment is paused, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cost and drug side effects once made CD4-guided pauses look attractive: stop therapy, restart when immune counts fall. The large SMART trial then reported a surprise rise in cardiovascular events after treatment interruption.

The team measured metabolic and immune activation changes during such breaks in chronic HIV infection. Their aim was to show how a pause could raise heart risk. Data of this kind ended the fashion for planned breaks and still warn any strategy that lets the virus rebound.
plos-pone-0002121:
Anna Matynia, Stephan Anagnostaras, Brian Wiltgen, and co-authors reported a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008 about the genes behind long-lasting memory. Early steps in forming a memory were known to need genes tied to synapses and to the making of new proteins. Far less was known about the later stages, when memories settle in for the long term.

The team ran a large reverse genetic screen, testing many genes at once to see which ones mice need for remote memory. The screen picked out two genes that play a part in that later stage. The result gives memory research new leads on how the brain keeps old memories alive.
plos-pone-0002221:
Toyoaki Natsume and co-authors studied how fission yeast pass on the special packing of their centromeres, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Centromeres are the chromosome spots where the machinery of cell division grabs hold. Their chromatin, the packing of DNA with protein, is unusual and must be copied exactly each time DNA is replicated.

The team focused on Mcl1, a helper protein for DNA polymerase alpha, the enzyme that starts new DNA strands. They found Mcl1 is required to propagate centromere structures in fission yeast. The result links the basic copying machinery to the survival of the chromosome's most vital landmark.
plos-pone-0002321:
Ran Tao and Wayne Hancock studied why one class of T cells resists a death signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nur77 is a nuclear receptor that pushes young T cells to die during the selection that removes self-reactive cells. It may also act in mature T cells out in the body. Regulatory T cells, marked by Foxp3, are the immune system's peacekeepers.

The team reports that these regulatory cells resist Nur77-induced apoptosis, and that the resistance promotes the survival of transplanted organs in their models. If peacekeeper cells are built to survive death signals, boosting that trait might help transplants last without heavy drugs.
plos-pone-0002421:
Bilal, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Erhan Bilal, Raul Rabadan, Gabriela Alexe, among others. Its subject is mitochondrial DNA Haplogroup D4a Is a Marker for Extreme Longevity in Japan. The team reports results from full mitochondrial DNA sequences taken from 112 Japanese semi-supercentenarians.

Each person in that group was aged above 105 years, and the data were combined with published results from older adults. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002521:
Elisaphenko and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Eugeny A. Elisaphenko, Nikolay N. Kolesnikov, Alexander I. Shevchenko, among others. Its subject is a Dual Origin of the Xist Gene from a Protein-Coding Gene and a Set of Transposable Elements. X-chromosome inactivation, which occurs in female eutherian mammals is controlled by a complex X-linked locus termed the X-inactivation center (XIC).

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002621:
In 2008, Eunsoo Kim and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about EEF2 analysis challenges the monophyly of archaeplastida and chromalveolata. Authorship is credited in the record to Eunsoo Kim and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Classification of eukaryotes provides a fundamental phylogenetic framework for ecological, medical, and industrial research. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002721:
Emmanuelle Wilhelm and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of TAF6δ controls apoptosis and gene expression in the absence of p53. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Emmanuelle Wilhelm, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Life and death decisions of metazoan cells hinge on the balance between the expression of pro- versus anti-apoptotic gene products. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002821:
In 2008, Josiah Johnston and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was quantitative image analysis reveals distinct structural transitions during aging in caenorhabditis elegans tissues. The catalog record names Josiah Johnston first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Aging is associated with functional and structural declines in many body systems, even in the absence of underlying disease. A further point appears in the abstract. In particular, skeletal muscles experience severe declines during aging, a phenomenon termed sarcopenia. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002921:
Roger Brookes, Philip Hill, Patrick Owiafe and colleagues tested a candidate tuberculosis vaccine in West Africa in 2008. The vaccine, MVA85A, uses a modified virus to carry antigen 85A from the tuberculosis germ. It had raised strong cellular immune responses in volunteers in the United Kingdom.

The PLOS ONE trial assessed safety and immune response in West African volunteers, a group closer to those most at risk of tuberculosis. Testing in the target region matters, since prior exposure and background infections can change vaccine effects. The study is an early step in judging this vaccine where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0003021:
Wangsheng Zhu, Zhongpeng Fan, Chao Zhang and co-authors mapped a puberty timing locus in mice in 2008. Pubertal timing starts when the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis switches back on, and both genes and environment modulate it. Inbred mouse strains differ in vaginal opening age, suggesting genetic background contributes.

A whole genome scan plus refined congenic strain analysis found a dominant X-linked region controlling that timing, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, locating the region on the X chromosome narrows the gene hunt. The work informs study of early and delayed puberty in mammals generally. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003121:
Marta Mastroianni, Kazuo Watanabe, Travis B. White and colleagues present this 2008 PLOS ONE work on a gene targeting tool drawn from mobile group II introns. These introns can insert themselves at exact sites in DNA by a process called retrohoming. In that process the cut-out intron RNA splices back into a DNA strand and is then copied by a protein the intron itself codes for.

The authors study how these reactions work in eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus. Readers learn the steps that let introns move and settle at chosen DNA sites. The work matters because such systems could be shaped into tools for precise gene targeting.
plos-pone-0003221:
Cristianne R. M. Frazier, Peggy Mason, Xiaoxi Zhuang and colleagues test early sugar exposure in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The cause of the current rise in obesity in western nations is poorly understood but is often attributed to a thrifty genotype, an evolutionary predisposition to store calories in times of plenty. In modern industrial environments, that thrift may backfire.

The authors test whether sucrose exposure in early life alters adult motivation and weight gain, as the title states. Readers see development, not just adult diet, put on trial. Early feeding effects would matter for how childhood nutrition advice is framed.
plos-pone-0003321:
Eric Hatterer, Monique Touret, Marie-Françoise Belin and colleagues track dendritic cells from spinal fluid in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In many neuroinflammatory diseases, dendritic cells build up in several parts of the central nervous system, including the cerebrospinal fluid. Myeloid dendritic cells invading the inflamed central nervous system are thus thought to play a major role. Their role covers both the start and the long course of inflammation.

The title reports that cerebrospinal fluid dendritic cells infiltrate the brain parenchyma and target the cervical lymph nodes when the nervous system is inflamed. Readers follow a route from fluid to brain to lymph node. That route may carry antigens that sustain diseases like multiple sclerosis.
plos-pone-0007421: Jessica A. Wray, Mary C. Sugden, Darryl C. Zeldin, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on an enzyme and a nuclear receptor. The enzyme is CYP2J2, one of the epoxygenases that make signaling fats from arachidonic acid. The receptor is PPAR alpha, a nuclear receptor that controls fat metabolism genes. Their title reports that CYP2J2 activates PPAR alpha in laboratory tests and in living systems, linking fat-derived signals to gene control.
plos-pone-0007521:
Fei Cai and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on carboxysomes, tiny protein compartments inside many bacteria. A carboxysome wraps the carbon-fixing enzyme RubisCO in a thin protein shell. The shell holds carbon dioxide in, giving the enzyme a rich environment to work in. Five-sided proteins sit at the shell's corners, its vertices. The team tested whether those corner pieces are essential to the barrier.

Without the pentameric vertex proteins, the shell could not keep carbon dioxide from leaking. The corners are therefore not decoration; they seal the compartment. That design lesson comes from nature's own carbon-capture device. Engineers hoping to copy carboxysomes now know which parts cannot be skipped. The study also clarifies how a shell built from simple pieces achieves a tight seal. Form and function meet at the corners.
plos-pone-0007621:
Carolyn Riddell and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on insect immunity and the force of matchups. Field work in spineless animals shows the result of an infection hangs on the exact host and parasite pair. That fact clashes with the old view of insect immunity as broad and blunt. The team measured which defenses insects raised across many host-parasite pairs. They asked whether the defenses called up hinge on who is fighting whom.

The pattern was pair by pair. Distinct pairs called up distinct sets of defenses. A blunt alarm would look the same each time; this one did not. Insects, it seems, tune their response more than books once allowed. That tuning reshapes how field scientists model disease in wild insects. It also counts for pest control with living agents, where the matchup decides who wins.
plos-pone-0007721:
Laura Hausmann and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the barn owl, a bird famed for pinpoint hearing. The owl's face is ringed by a ruff of stiff feathers. That ruff shapes the sound that reaches each ear.

The authors tested the ruff's role by removing it in a virtual model. Without the ruff, the owl's ability to locate sounds dropped. The test shows the facial ruff works like a built-in dish for hearing. It sharpens the cues the owl uses to hunt prey in total darkness.
plos-pone-0007821:
Elisabeth Frank and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It improves protein measurement in mouse models of mental illness. Finding which proteins change in such models is essential for understanding disease. Mass spectrometry is the leading tool for comparing protein levels.

To make comparisons exact, scientists label tissues with heavy isotopes. The team fed mice bacteria enriched with heavy nitrogen, isotope 15N. The novel diet labels the animals' own proteins from within. Their method sharpens proteomic analyses of the brain. Better measurements give psychiatric research a firmer base.
plos-pone-0007921:
William Monahan published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It builds a mechanistic model of where species can live as seasons change. Niche theory guides how scientists predict species' responses to climate change. A species' realized niche depends on its neighbors, while its fundamental niche is set by physiology.

Monahan's model starts from that physiology instead of from past sightings. It measures how distributions should shift across seasonal temperature gradients. Models grounded in mechanism can extrapolate to climates never seen before. That is exactly what climate forecasts demand. The work offers conservation a sharper predictive tool.
plos-pone-0008021:
David Gunn and colleagues asked why some women look young for their years, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A vast trade sells creams and treatments on that wish, yet the true drivers of a youthful face were untested. Twins offered a way to split nature from habit.

Comparing twins and other women, the team weighed which face traits set guessed age and how much genes counted against sun, smoke, and other habits. Both sides mattered, but not evenly for every trait. The work gives buyers and makers a sober map of what can, and cannot, be bought in a jar.
plos-pone-0008121:
Kevin Yip and colleagues rebuilt computer gene networks more truly by joining two data kinds in PLOS ONE in 2010. The DREAM3 contest asks teams to infer how genes control each other inside a simulated cell. Two data kinds were on offer: readings from strains with one gene deleted, and readings over time after a push.

Each kind alone left gaps in the map. Joined, they let the team draw the clostest match to the hidden true network in the contest. The lesson is plain for real biology too: kinds of data that seem spare apart can be rich together.
plos-pone-0008221:
Clive Bate and colleagues tested a diabetes drug against prion disease in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Prion diseases turn a normal host protein into a misfolded, harmful form. That harmful form builds up in the brain. Its spread is tied to synapse loss and nerve cell death. Few treatments exist for these fatal diseases.

The drug glimepiride lowered expression of the normal prion protein in their tests. It also prevented formation of the disease form. Cells were protected against prion-mediated toxicity as a result. The findings suggest a common drug class might be worth exploring further.
plos-pone-0008321:
Philip Bejon and colleagues studied malaria and bed nets in children in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Insecticide-treated nets reduce a child's exposure to malaria. Less exposure should cut disease, but may also slow the building of immunity. Long-term data after community-wide net distribution show sustained benefits overall. Common practice, though, varies in who uses nets and when.

The team found that age and net use interact to set risk. Febrile malaria risk depended on both factors together. That nuance matters for targeting protection to the most vulnerable children. It also informs how net programs are evaluated.
plos-pone-0008421:
Long Nam Nguyen, David Trofa, and Joshua D. Nosanchuk studied a fungal pathogen in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Candida parapsilosis is a yeast that infects humans. Its fatty acid synthase is built from two subunits encoded by Fas1 and Fas2. The team deleted the Fas2 genes using a modified genetic technique. The gene proved essential in media lacking fatty acids.

Fatty acid synthase thus impacts the pathobiology of this fungus. It mattered both in vitro and during mammalian infection. An essential enzyme is a candidate drug target. Blocking fat synthesis could weaken a pathogen that resists other drugs.
plos-pone-0008521:
Robert Holman and co-authors survey prion diseases in the United States in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Prion diseases are rare, progressive brain disorders in humans and animals. The most common human form is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or CJD. It occurs worldwide at low rates. Variant CJD is a newer form linked to animal disease. It emerged as a zoonosis, an infection passed from animals. The team summarize US cases and patterns.

Their survey covers incidence, demographics, and disease forms nationwide. Such surveillance helps detect new clusters or a rise in variant cases. Prion diseases are always fatal, so early detection matters for blood and tissue safety. The paper gives a national baseline for the United States.
plos-pone-0008621:
Annie J. Sasco, Antoine Jaquet, Emilie Boidin, and co-authors published a global health review in PLOS ONE in 2010. Strong drug combinations had begun letting people with HIV live much longer. In wealthy countries, that longer life came with a higher risk of cancer. The authors asked what the same shift would mean for sub-Saharan Africa.

They weighed what was known about cancers tied to AIDS across the region. They also looked ahead, asking how wider drug access and longer lives might change that burden. Cancer care there often starts late, with few tools to treat it. Their review frames planning needs early, before clinics face a wave they cannot handle.
plos-pone-0008721:
Rogério Rosada, Ana Moreira, Fabiani Frantz, and colleagues tested whether prior immunity blunts a lung drug. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug joins human IL-13 to a weakened bacterial toxin. It aims at cells that drive lung scarring, or fibrosis. Patients may already carry immunity to that toxin from past exposures. Such immunity could disarm the drug before it works.

Mice with immunity to the toxin still gained protection from lung fibrosis. The drug's benefit survived the immune memory against one part. That survival keeps the treatment idea alive for real patients with similar immunity.
plos-pone-0008821:
Yosuke Ichijima, Ken-ichi Yoshioka, Yoshiko Yoshioka, and colleagues linked copy stress in DNA to doubled genomes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early tumor cells gain immortality while their genomes grow unstable. How that instability starts on its own was elusive. Oncogenes can force cells to copy DNA too fast. That rush, called replication stress, leaves lesions behind.

Lesions from copy stress triggered errors during cell division. Some daughter cells ended with twice the normal chromosome set. Tetraploid cells are a known stepping stone to cancer chaos. The route ties a common early stress to genome doubling.
plos-pone-0008921:
Isabelle Mouro-Chanteloup, Sylvie Cochet, Mohamed Chami, and colleagues rebuilt a human ammonia channel inside artificial bubbles. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rh proteins move ammonium across cell membranes throughout the body. The human member RhCG works in kidney and other tissues. Studying a membrane channel in isolation requires a clean setting. Liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, provide exactly that. Purified protein must first be made and kept stable.

Inserted into liposomes, the purified RhCG channel worked. Ammonium crossed the bubble walls through the rebuilt channel. A working rebuild proves the protein alone suffices for transport. The system now allows precise tests of channel mechanics.
plos-pone-0009021:
Anders Larsen and Søren-Peter Olesen mixed two channel versions to copy the heart's real electrical current, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A current called IKr helps reset the heartbeat after each contraction. It flows through channels built from the ERG1 protein. Two forms of that protein, ERG1a and ERG1b, were both suspected contributors.

Natural IKr varies oddly in speed from cell to cell. Expressing the two forms in different ratios reproduced that variety. The blend also changed the shape of the heart cell's electrical cycle. The heart's current, it seems, is a duet rather than a solo.
plos-pone-0009121:
Lorelei Shoemaker and co-authors listed proteins that set young brain progenitors apart from older ones, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain grows from a mixed pool of neural stem and progenitor cells. The differences inside that pool are poorly charted. Markers distinguishing the cell types would sharpen brain development research.

The team compared proteins in mouse cortical progenitors. Embryonic and postnatal cells carried measurably different protein sets. Some differences likely run migration, growth, or fate choice. A parts list for each age helps labs isolate the cells they need.
plos-pone-0009221:
Jan Spanholtz and co-authors published this cancer therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can attack tumors. Giving them to patients is a promising extra treatment for many cancers. The catch is numbers: therapy needs huge counts of working cells, grown under clinical rules.

The team built a method to grow them from umbilical cord blood. They started from CD34-positive stem cells found in that blood. Their protocol expanded the killer cells by very large, log-scale amounts while keeping them functional. A reliable supply like this is what adoptive cell therapy needs to reach more patients.
plos-pone-0009321:
Vincent Zijnge and co-authors published this dental study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mouth is coated with biofilms, layered cities of bacteria on the teeth. Those films cause gum disease and tooth decay. They also serve scientists as a handy model for how biofilms grow and resist antibiotics.

The team examined the architecture of oral biofilms on natural teeth. They mapped how the layers are arranged and which bacteria sit where. Structure explains much of a biofilm's toughness, since sheltered cells survive attacks. Knowing the layout of the real thing, on real teeth, grounds the models built in dishes.
plos-pone-0011421:
Amir Nia and co-authors showed in 2010 that a gene variant can predict how well a heart rhythm drug works. Flecainide steadies the heart in atrial fibrillation, a common rhythm disorder, yet patients respond unevenly for reasons doctors could not see. The team tested whether variation in the gene for a heart adrenaline receptor explained the difference.

Patients carrying a particular form of the receptor gene responded to the drug differently from those without it. A simple genetic test could therefore help doctors choose who should get this drug and who should try another first. That is the promise of personalized prescribing: less trial and error with drugs that carry real side effects. The study is a step toward heart care in which the prescription is matched to the patient's genes from the start.
plos-pone-0011521:
Eugenia Villa-Cuesta, Brian Sage, and Marc Tatar examined in 2010 how a survival protein keeps being made while fruit flies fast. The protein dFoxO helps cells weather hunger, and fasting normally shuts down most protein production to save energy. The puzzle is how the cell keeps producing this one protector while the general machinery idles.

The answer lies in special landing pads within the protein's own message, internal ribosome entry sites in its head region, which let production continue during fasting. That workaround reveals a priority system: survival instructions jump the queue when food runs out. The mechanism is a neat example of cells planning for hard times inside the design of a single gene. It may also hint at how tumor cells, which often fast in poorly fed tissue, keep their own protectors flowing.
plos-pone-0011621:
Liu Yang and co-authors developed a way to measure cell stress in living tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells react to a build-up of unfolded proteins in a compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum. This unfolded protein response is a key defence and is tied to many human diseases, yet its true level in the body was hard to gauge.

Their method uses a chemical tag that captures a key stress signal, revealing how much strain cells are under in normal conditions. The measurements show how close healthy cells run to their limits. Better measures of this stress should help research on diabetes, liver disease and other linked illnesses.
plos-pone-0011721:
Xuhua Guan and co-authors reviewed three decades of pneumonia research on mainland China, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pneumonia is a leading infectious killer worldwide, but China's share of that burden was unclear, because much of the data sits in Chinese-language journals that international reviews miss.

The team systematically searched both Chinese and English literature from 1985 to 2008 for primary data on pneumonia occurrence and deaths. Combining both sources gives the first clear measure of the disease's toll in China. That baseline is essential for judging vaccines and treatment programmes there.
plos-pone-0011821:
Brandon Beagle and Gail Johnson studied a loose piece of a signal protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Wnt pathway is a master control route that guides cell growth and cell fate, so its output is kept under tight control at many levels. One of its parts is the receptor helper LRP6, which also has an inner piece that can float free in the cell.

The authors tested how that free piece, called LRP6-ICD, changes the work of the TCF/LEF-1 switches that turn Wnt target genes on. The piece tuned those switches, in ways that shifted with context. A loose fragment acting as a dial adds a fresh layer of control to a famous route.
plos-pone-0011921:
Kathryn Butler and co-workers measured in 2010 how burn injury changes the movement of neutrophils, the white blood cells that rush to infections. Severe burns trigger a body-wide inflammatory storm and often end in sepsis. Earlier work had shown that neutrophils from burn patients are worse at homing in on targets.

Using microfluidic devices, tiny channels that steer cells through controlled chemical trails, the team found that burns reduce how fast neutrophils move in the right direction. Slower, less directed cells help explain the infection risk that haunts burn care. The device also offers a compact way to test drugs meant to restore immune cell movement.
plos-pone-0012021:
Joakim Ek and co-workers charted in 2010 how harm spreads through the spinal cord of the rat after a bruise-type injury. The first blow is just the start; a second wave of harm grows for weeks, and the cell steps that drive it are not clear. The team took stock of the wound's size and of how much of each cord tissue was left, from as early as a quarter of an hour to ten weeks on.

That time line shows when the cord's grey core and its white fiber tracts are lost, and where the loss halts. The two tissues do not fail on the same clock. A map with timing tells drug and cell trials when they must act to save each tissue, a point that has sunk more than one past trial.
plos-pone-0012121:
Lin Cui, Kenoki Ohuchida, Kazuhiro Mizumoto, and co-authors compared types of colon cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. They also studied the fibroblasts that grow alongside tumors, since cancer cells do not live alone. One surface marker divides colon cancer cells into two groups, and a second marker picks out a set of tumor-linked fibroblasts the team isolated directly from tissue.

The marked fibroblasts interacted much more strongly with one cancer cell group than with the other. Such pairings may help certain cancer cells grow or spread, fed by the support cells around them. Naming the strongest partnerships points to new places where treatment might cut the tumor off from its helpers.
plos-pone-0012221:
Sangeetha M, Vaijayanti Kale, and Lalita Limaye worked to grow blood stem cells from umbilical cord blood in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cord blood can cure blood diseases through transplant, but one unit holds too few stem cells for many patients. Growing the cells in a dish should fix that, yet the expansion process itself tires the cells out and weakens their later performance.

Adding either of two protective compounds during expansion kept the cells fitter in lab tests and better at settling into recipient mice afterward. Healthier expanded cells could stretch each cord blood unit to treat larger patients. The approach brings cord blood transplants closer to routine use for adults, not just children.
plos-pone-0012321:
Sabine Gollner, Barbara Riemer, Pedro Martínez Arbizu, and co-authors surveyed tiny seafloor animals at a deep-sea vent field in PLOS ONE in 2010. At nine degrees north on the East Pacific Rise, vents pour out fluids ranging from mild to extreme in heat, acidity, and sulfide. The meiofauna, animals smaller than grains of sand, live along that whole gradient in the trough where the vents sit.

Charting which species live at which harshness maps the true limits of animal life. Vent fields are now eyed for mining, so a baseline census tells us what would be lost and which refuges matter. The gradient itself is a natural laboratory for how life responds to worsening chemistry, including an acidifying ocean.
plos-pone-0012421:
Martin Kapun, Viola Nolte, Thomas Flatt and colleagues tested which fruit flies the Drosophila C virus can infect, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The virus is a common pathogen of lab flies and is well studied in two species. In the wild it may meet many hosts, and its true range shapes how it spreads and evolves.

The team exposed several fly species and found that infection success and harm varied widely by host. Some species resisted, while close relatives suffered. Host range data matter for using this virus as a model of insect disease and for judging risks if such viruses were ever used to control pest insects.
plos-pone-0012521:
Ethel Pereira, Nan Liao, Geoff Neale and colleagues studied how cell stress tunes vessel growth factors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When the cell's protein-folding factory, the endoplasmic reticulum, gets overloaded, the unfolded protein response switches on to restore order. Tumors live under such stress and still manage to summon blood vessels, a puzzle the team addressed.

They found the stress response regulates proangiogenic factors at two levels: the genes' transcription and the handling of their messages afterward. Two-level control lets stressed cells fine-tune vessel signals fast. The links may expose weak points where drugs can cut a tumor's blood supply.
plos-pone-0012621:
Rybina and Pasyukova studied a natural gene variant in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The gene, called Lim3, helps shape nerve cells early in life and matches a human gene pair known as LHX3 and LHX4. It had also been flagged as a gene that may change how long a fly lives.

Their 2010 work shows the variant alters how much Lim3 is switched on, and that this tracks with lifespan. One gene touching both brain growth and ageing makes it a rich case for study. Findings in flies often point to shared controls in other animals.
plos-pone-0012721:
Yue and Chang used DNA parentage tests to study mating in a freshwater shrimp, Caridina ensifera. Genetic parentage tools reveal who really fathers the young in a species. Among the huge crustacean group Malacostraca, mating systems were still mostly unstudied when they wrote in 2010.

Their tests found that females often carry young from several males at once, at high rates. Multiple paternity changes how we think about shrimp breeding and population genetics. It also gives fishery and conservation work a firmer base for this species group.  Field samples from wild shrimp ground the genetics in real mating life.
plos-pone-0012821:
Garcia-Gonzalez, Outeda, Zhou and co-authors showed that two kidney genes are also required to build a healthy placenta. Faults in PKD1 and PKD2 cause the common inherited kidney disease in which cysts grow and kidneys fail. Their 2010 mouse study removed these genes and watched development beyond the kidney.

Embryos lacking them failed to form a normal placenta, the organ that feeds the unborn young. A placenta role widens the known reach of these genes in development. It may also explain some pregnancy losses tied to this gene family.
pmc-2375021:
Huang, Sherman, Tan, and co-authors present the DAVID gene functional classification tool. Modern experiments often yield lists of hundreds of genes with no clear story. DAVID uses a fuzzy grouping method to condense such lists into organised classes of related genes, which the authors call biological modules.

Grouping by shared function helps researchers see themes instead of noise: cell growth, immunity, or other joint roles. The module-centred approach differs from tools that rank genes one by one. For labs facing a long gene list, a clear grouping is often the first real clue about what an experiment changed.
pmc-2746121:
Terwilliger and Berendzen present a fully automated procedure for solving crystal structures by MAD and MIR methods. Those methods use special X-ray signals to find atomic positions in a crystal. Hand solving was slow and depended heavily on expert judgement at each step.

Their scheme turns structure solution into an optimisation problem, scored step by step by computer. Automation let more structures be solved, faster, by less specialised users. The work helped shift crystallography from a craft bottleneck toward a routine pipeline, feeding the rapid growth of known protein shapes.
pmc-3618321:
Hänzelmann, Castelo, and Guinney present GSVA, a method for gene set variation analysis of microarray and RNA-Seq data. Gene set analysis condenses expression profiles into summaries of pathways or signatures. Compared with single-gene analysis, it reduces noise and the sheer number of results, and adds biological interpretability.

GSVA estimates how much each pathway varies in each individual sample, rather than only comparing groups. Sample-level scores let researchers tie pathway activity to clinical traits directly. The method is widely used in cancer studies to characterise tumours one patient at a time.
pmc-4015721:
IntHout, Ioannidis, and Borm compared two methods for meta-analysis in 2014. Meta-analysis pools results from many trials of the same question to get a clearer answer. The standard DerSimonian-Laird method is used almost everywhere for random effects models.

The authors show that the standard method often gives error rates that are too high. A less used method, named for Hartung, Knapp, Sidik, and Jonkman, performs far better in their tests. It is also simple to apply in practice. Their work gives trial reviewers a strong reason to switch methods, so pooled results are less likely to claim effects that are not real.
pmc-4053721:
Law, Chen, Shi, and their co-authors presented the voom method in 2014 for RNA sequencing data. RNA-seq counts how many times each gene's message is read in a sample. Those counts need care before standard linear models, built for other data types, can be used on them.

Voom charts how the spread of the log counts changes with their size, then gives each data point a weight based on its precision. Those weights enter the limma framework, a trusted set of tools for gene studies. The method lets labs use mature linear model tools on RNA-seq counts, with results that respect how noisy each count is.
pmc-4284921:
Collins, Reitsma, Altman, and their colleagues issued the TRIPOD Statement in 2015. Prediction models help health providers estimate the risk that a disease is present or that an event will occur later. Such models guide real decisions, so their reports must be clear and complete.
