TRIPOD lists what a report of a prediction model should include, for both diagnosis and prognosis models. Poor reporting had made many models hard to judge or reuse. A shared standard lets readers check how a model was built and tested. That improves trust in risk tools used at the bedside and in clinics.
plos-pone-0359421: Chen and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on predicting where vocational college graduates will work. Their model uses the XGBoost method, tuned by a search method called TPE. It aims for fine-grained guesses about each student's employment destination. Colleges in China could use such forecasts to guide career advice and to show how well their programs place students.
plos-pone-0359321: Jiang and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on guessing body poses in 3D from images. Their framework, HADD, is aware of body hierarchy and splits the pose into parts before cleaning the result. A denoising step works over space and time at once. Better pose tracking helps animation, sports analysis, and robots that need to follow human movement safely.
plos-pone-0358221: Kang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a trial on cleaner air for children with asthma. The AIRVAC study will test home ventilation and air cleaners in four parallel groups. Families are assigned at random in this controlled trial. Home air is one asthma trigger parents can change, so a four-way test can show which fix, or pair of fixes, truly helps.
plos-pone-0357821:
Francesca Genovese, Martina Fanghella, Corrado Sinigaglia, and Guido Barchiesi revisit a basic question about how people copy each other, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Watching someone move tends to prime the same movement in the observer, a reflex called automatic imitation. One leading theory says the reflex is learned, built from paired seeing and doing. If so, training people to respond against what they see should weaken it.

The team measured the reflex before and after such counter training at several time points, expecting it to fade if learned pairings drive it. It did not fade significantly at any tested point. That stubbornness challenges the learning account, at least in its current form, and pushes the debate toward mechanisms that training alone cannot rewrite. The study is a useful reminder that a tidy theory of imitation still faces contrary evidence.

plos-pone-0356621:
Sancho Pedro Xavier led a team of eight authors who used machine learning on cancer records from Mato Grosso, Brazil, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. They linked the state cancer registry with death records for women diagnosed with breast cancer. The aim was to predict which women face the highest risk of dying.

Xavier's models sorted patients by risk and pointed to the factors that drive that risk. In a state with vast distances and limited clinics, such sorting can help direct scarce follow-up care to the women who need it most. The study also shows what linked public records, handled with care, can teach a health system about its own gaps.
plos-pone-0358321:
Debbie Johnson led a team of eight authors who studied NHS staff in England after pregnancy or newborn loss at work, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Midwives, nurses, and doctors who care for grieving parents carry their own grief, often with little support. The team used a qualitative approach, listening closely to staff accounts.

Johnson's group recorded what staff say helps, such as peer support, time to recover, and simple acknowledgment, and what is missing. Those findings give hospital leaders concrete steps rather than vague calls for resilience. Services that support their own carers protect both staff retention and the quality of care that bereaved families receive at their worst moments.
plos-pone-0353021:
Qian Wu led a team of six authors reviewing AI for a puzzling lung pattern, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The pattern, called PRISm, shows a preserved ratio with impaired spirometry readings, a gray zone in lung testing. Clinicians disagree on what it means and who needs follow-up, so AI tools have been proposed to help.

Wu's review gathered those AI applications and judged where the evidence stands. It maps where algorithms genuinely aid reading of lung tests, and where claims outrun proof. That candor helps doctors decide what to trust now and what to await. It also tells developers which gaps, such as wider patient testing, they must fill before clinics should rely on their tools.
plos-pone-0357921:
Müfide Arzu Özkarafakılı and three colleagues studied a hidden burden of lung disease in women, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease steals breath over years, and intimacy often suffers quietly alongside. The team measured sexual dysfunction in women with COPD and linked it to how heavy their overall symptom burden is.

Özkarafakılı's study brings a cost of lung disease into the clinical conversation where it belongs. Doctors rarely ask, and patients rarely raise it, so the problem stays untreated. Evidence of a link with symptom burden gives clinicians a reason to ask and a guide to who may need help most. Quality of life in chronic disease includes private life, and this work insists on counting it.
plos-pone-0356721:
Gary Duclos led a large team, including the EUROBACT-2 Study Group, examining steroid use in sepsis, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Whether steroids help sepsis patients is one of intensive care's fiercest debates. The team studied patients whose sepsis came with bloodstream infections picked up in hospital, and linked hydrocortisone use to their outcomes.

Duclos's ancillary analysis uses a large existing cohort, adding real-world nuance to trial evidence. It asks when steroids help and when they harm, a question bedside doctors face nightly. Hospital-acquired infections are among the hardest sepsis cases, so evidence in exactly this group is valuable. The study will not end the debate, but it sharpens it with data from real wards.
plos-pone-0354121:
Peixue Liu and coauthors published a 2026 computer vision paper in PLOS ONE on clearing haze from satellite images. Haze dulls the images that land-use mapping and change detection depend on, washing out detail and color. Their network, DEMANet, processes the image through three shrinking stages: early layers use a dual-path module to protect fine detail. Deep layers use two-level attention to grasp the whole scene and haze pattern. A cross-stage module uses edges and color differences to locate haze and ferry detail between stages.

On widely used public remote sensing datasets, the network beat existing dehazing algorithms while keeping intricate detail and faithful color. The authors attribute the gains to the division of labor: local branches guard texture, attention guards global consistency, and the haze-guided links stop information leaking away during reconstruction. Cleaner satellite imagery feeds directly into better environmental monitoring and land management.
plos-pone-0349721:
Shantengyue Jiang and Mo Zhang offer a 2026 modeling paper on gas moving through hot, cracked coal deep underground. Older work often treated crack roughness in rough terms, which made danger forecasts for mines less useful. Their model links heat, water pressure, rock strain, and crack shape in one system, using a single roughness score to connect surface bumps with how easily gas flows.

Checks against real records from a Liupanshui coal face and from a gas well support the model. Warmer coal and smoother cracks both let gas move faster and raised pressure and ground shift in the tests. Mine teams can use results like these to judge where gas may gather before it becomes a hazard.
plos-pone-0350921:
Carolina Vivas-Valencia and colleagues model where Zimbabwe should place bedside infant HIV test machines to do the most good. Babies born to mothers with HIV need virus testing within weeks, and distant central labs delay answers and treatment. In one southern province, clinics number more than a hundred. There the team linked a detailed child HIV simulation with a placement optimizer. It tested current locations against the best possible ones, for life expectancy and value.

Most existing machines moved to better-chosen clinics in the best layout. A few stayed in place. That layout sharply raised the share of infants getting results within a month. It also raised the share starting treatment within a month. Life expectancy for infected infants rose by more than a year in the best layout. Vivas-Valencia and colleagues argue placement, not just purchase, decides what these machines deliver.
plos-pone-0356821:
Mahmoud S Abdallah, Rania Mahafdeh, and Rima Hisham Shakhatreh tested one simple idea. Could a single short training session improve how Jordan's local pharmacists handle asthma? Their 2026 study enrolled 110 licensed pharmacists. It measured their asthma knowledge, attitudes, and inhaler technique. Then came a two-hour session based on treatment guidelines. Two weeks later, the team measured everything again.

Scores rose across the board after training. The gains covered knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practice with both common inhaler types. Pharmacists with higher pharmacy degrees started ahead of those with first degrees. Pharmacists are often the health workers asthma patients can reach most easily. So the study supports brief, focused refreshers as a cheap way to lift day-to-day asthma care.
plos-pone-0357021:
Chetwynd Osborne, D Huy Dang, Soyini Mc Pherson, and Shaun A Watmough traced mercury through the forests and streams of Guyana. Mercury is the toxic metal released by small-scale gold mining. The team compared its ratio to carbon in leaves, litter, soil, water, and sediment. The comparison set was twenty-five studies worldwide. Their 2026 study used carbon as the yardstick because mercury rides on carbon through ecosystems.

The pattern of movement matched the global picture. Mercury builds as leaves fall and decay, then travels toward streams. But near Guyanese mines the ratios ran far above world averages. That confirms heavy local loading from the air. The comparison also suggests wetlands worldwide quietly feed mercury into surface waters. It is a route managers of mining regions should watch.
plos-pone-0346921:
Rachel Lara Green and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for filming the electrical conversation between a preschool teacher's brain and a child's during shared tasks. The study uses dual brain recording, called hyperscanning. Teacher and child work on literacy, problem solving, and self-control activities. The tasks are designed to reveal how teachers scaffold. Scaffolding is the moment-by-moment support that builds a child's executive functions.

Researchers will measure how tightly behavior and brain activity synchronize. They will relate synchrony to each partner's own executive skills and intelligence. The child's measured school readiness counts too. Parent-child synchrony is well studied. Teachers, who increasingly share early care worldwide, are not. Findings could shape how preschool teachers are trained to pitch their help.
plos-pone-0343321:
Laure Peyro-Saint-Paul and colleagues surveyed the French public about a delicate ethics question: should people who volunteer for drug trials be paid, and how much? Their 2026 exploratory study gathered sixty-five respondents in clinics and online, presented three fictional trials varying in risk, burden, and personal benefit, and asked what compensation seemed fair.

Three quarters backed payment in principle. The strongest triggers were facing a new experimental drug, invasive procedures, and lost income. Support and suggested amounts rose with burden: highest for a demanding, uncertain trial with some benefit, lowest for an easy one. The survey feeds a larger French project building a decision tool so sponsors and ethics committees price participation fairly without dangling coercive sums.
plos-pone-0354921:
Junkang Ren and three colleagues present a deep learning system for reverse-engineering how computer protocols behave, in this 2026 paper. Security analysts often face private or undocumented protocols and must infer their internal state machines, the rules for which message can follow which, from observed traffic alone. Their framework pairs a sequence model called Mamba with a graph learning method.

The system first extracts deep features from message exchanges, builds an initial map of protocol states, then merges redundant states in a data-driven way rather than by fixed rules. Tested on five protocols, from web and email traffic to industrial control protocols, it recovered state machine structures accurately and predicted behavior better than mainstream alternatives. Removing either main component hurt performance, confirming both contribute. The authors offer it as a sharper tool for protocol analysis and security testing.
plos-pone-0351421:
Xuemei Xu and four colleagues study how live-streamed selling builds trust in an unlikely product, durian, in this 2026 marketing study. Durian is expensive, perishable, and famously pungent, so buying it unseen from a phone stream is a leap of faith. The researchers interviewed buyers of durian sold through Douyin livestreams, then surveyed more than four hundred verified purchasers to test what drove their buying.

Four features of the streaming scene stood out: visual signs of freshness, the streamer's expertise, real-time interaction, and a wish to support rural farmers. Freshness cues and expertise built trust, which in turn drove impulse buying. Interaction and farmer support worked differently, by making the experience enjoyable; the good feeling of helping farmers itself acted as a pleasure that encouraged purchase. The authors offer the model to regional farm brands going digital.
plos-pone-0356421:
Mairobys Socorro and three colleagues set up a goat model for studying jaw joint degeneration, in this 2026 paper. The temporomandibular joint, which hinges the jaw, can develop osteoarthritis, but its cartilage is a fibrous type unlike that in knees. Therapies therefore need testing in a large animal with a similar joint. The team surgically created two kinds of bone-and-cartilage defects in the goat jaw joint and compared how they healed.

Neither defect type healed properly over two months: the holes filled with fibrous tissue and rough new bone at the edges, with no new cartilage, and the surrounding cartilage showed arthritic changes. Because both behaved alike, the authors favor the tunnel-style defect, which spares the joint disc and needs less surgical disturbance while producing larger defects. The model gives regenerative medicine a realistic testbed for future jaw therapies.
plos-pone-0355721:
Dorcas Kalaba and co-authors reviewed outcomes for drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment across Zambia over five years. Success rates sat below the global target, and national evidence on who fares worst was thin. Their 2026 study drew programme records for more than twelve hundred patients treated in all ten provinces.

About two thirds of patients finished with a favourable outcome. Normal body weight more than doubled the odds of success compared with underweight patients. Two provinces, Muchinga and Western, showed markedly lower success odds than the rest. Kalaba and colleagues argue food support and province-targeted fixes are essential if Zambia is to close its resistant-TB outcome gap.
plos-pone-0355621:
Wondaya Fenta Zewdia and co-authors modelled home birth and under-five child death together in Ethiopia. Both outcomes remain common and may share roots, so studying them jointly sharpens the picture. Their 2026 analysis used a national mini survey of more than five thousand women with a birth history.

About half of the women had delivered at home, and about one in twenty reported losing a child under five. The two outcomes were significantly linked: home delivery came with more than double the odds of a child death experience. Schooling, wealth, pregnancy care, and media exposure lowered both risks, while rural living raised them. The authors urge combined action on access, education, and care visits.
plos-pone-0354521:
Rebecca Muñiz and co-authors used oysters from the Texas Gulf Coast as early warning sensors for plastic pollution. Oysters filter feed, so microplastics collect in their tissues. Their 2026 study sampled sixty oysters at two field sites and compared them with oysters held two weeks in clean water.

Field oysters carried many plastic fibres, mostly polyethylene, in gills and digestive glands. Clean-water oysters held notably smaller particles, supporting the warning idea. Tissue checks showed raised markers of protein damage and shifted antioxidant defences where plastics were present. Muñiz and colleagues propose oyster chemistry as a cheap sentinel for coastal contamination before wider harm shows.
plos-pone-0349121:
Alexandra Linz and co-authors built data-driven rules to find Lyme disease cases inside electronic health records. In regions where Lyme is common, fast and accurate case finding would serve clinics and researchers alike. Their 2026 study used records from one health system and tested algorithms built only from structured, easily pulled fields.

Diagnosis codes, laboratory orders and results, demographics, and antibiotic orders all carried signal. A hand-built decision tree performed best. It required a Lyme code, a positive antibody test, and a doxycycline order close in time, in combination. That rule reached solid accuracy with high sensitivity. Linz and colleagues say such simple logic could anchor automated surveillance after wider testing.
plos-pone-0353121:
Thirada Srinil and colleagues run in 2026 a blinded trial for people having keyhole shoulder surgery, comparing two drugs added to a nerve block near the neck. One added drug was a sedative type agent given at a high dose, and the other was a steroid. Neither patients nor assessors knew which was used, and pain relief time was the main measure.

Both mixes gave similar time before pain returned, though the sedative mix kept feeling and movement blocked a bit longer. Pain scores, extra painkillers, and satisfaction matched. Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and sleepiness occurred more often with the sedative mix, but all passed without intensive care.
plos-pone-0336321:
Bijaya Niraula and colleagues survey in 2026 women who live in a slum area in a municipality near Kathmandu, Nepal, about care during monthly periods. Several hundred women of reproductive age answered a tested questionnaire chosen through systematic sampling. Questions covered products used, washing, bathing, and social restrictions faced at home and in the community.

About half used disposable pads and many used reusable cloth. Almost all faced some restriction during periods, and more than half felt treated as impure. Schooling and income linked to awareness, while job and ethnic group linked to handwashing. The authors call for better water, toilets, and teaching that tackles stigma.
plos-pone-0355221:
Ashwini Kumar and co-authors design in 2026 a compact four part antenna shaped with a spider like pattern for advanced fifth generation wireless use. Multiple antennas working together need to stay small, cover a wide band, and avoid interfering with each other. Learning methods helped tune the design, with one method giving the most accurate predictions.

A built sample matched the design goals, covering a broad range of frequencies below the higher bands with good gain and strong separation between parts. Standard checks for linked antenna performance passed. The authors present the antenna as a candidate for future fast wireless gear, including early sixth generation work.
plos-pone-0354021:
Hamed Nejat, Jason Sherfey, and André Bastos introduce in 2026 an evolutionary method for tuning spiking brain models that aim to explain how the brain predicts incoming signals. Such models can produce real brain rhythms, but setting their many connection values by hand is slow. Their genetic search adjusts values automatically against goals such as firing rates and the balance between fast and slower rhythms.

Tests moved from simple cases to recordings from monkey visual cortex, where the method reproduced recorded rhythm patterns tied to prediction. A second neuron model gave similar success, showing the search is not tied to one setup. The authors frame it as a tool, not proof of the theory.
plos-pone-0352021:
Muhammad Farooq and co-authors propose in 2026 a blockchain system to track sugarcane from field to factory and rebuild trust among farmers, traders, and officials. Hidden dealings and fake shortages cut farmer earnings and strain national economies in their account. Their design uses smart contracts, a dedicated digital token for payments, and a decentralised file system for private records.

Tests reported faster block handling, higher transaction capacity, and lower costs than rival supply chain projects they compared. A public coin launch is suggested to fund the system long term. The work is a design and test study, not a report of a live national rollout.
plos-pone-0354721:
Sudip Saha and four colleagues published this 2026 engineering paper on predicting how much working life a machine has left. Their model pairs convolutional layers, which spot local wear patterns, with memory networks that follow slow decline over time. It was tested on construction machines, steel casting equipment, and lithium batteries.

The combined model beat rival methods on all three data sets, cutting prediction error notably against older approaches. Light retraining helped it move between machine types. Saha presents the single framework as a practical base for maintenance planning across very different industries.
plos-pone-0354821:
Linyao Peng led a team of six authors on this 2026 study replacing hand counting with computer vision in worm reproduction tests. The tiny nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is a workhorse of aging and genetics research, but each mother can leave over a hundred offspring to count. They trained recent YOLO image models on nearly ten thousand brood photos.

The best model counted viable offspring with high accuracy against human counts, cutting months of microscope work to about two hours on a home graphics card. Peng shares the pipeline so other labs can adapt it to new image collections.
plos-pone-0353621:
Long and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, hunt for genes that help cervical cancer resist cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. Drug resistance is a major reason treatment fails. Their search through large cancer data sets singled out a gene called SPP1, which was turned up in tumor tissue.

Tests in cancer cells showed SPP1 levels were higher still in cells that had learned to resist cisplatin. Turning SPP1 down slowed cell growth, raised cell death, and made the drug work better. Turning it up did the opposite. The gene's effects ran in part through a second gene, KRAS: adjusting KRAS partly undid what SPP1 did to drug response. The authors propose that blocking the SPP1 to KRAS path could help restore the power of chemotherapy. The evidence so far comes from data sets and cells, not patients.
plos-pone-0353721:
Muhammad Hussien and three colleagues survey Egyptian farming households on whether failing land pushes people to move away, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Salt creeping into soil is shrinking harvests across Egypt. Nearly eighteen hundred respondents answered questions on land condition, income, and migration wishes, and the team modelled the answers through a theory of how people weigh threats and their ability to respond.

More than a third had seen their land's productivity fall within a decade, and over a fifth were actively seeking to relocate, mostly to Cairo or abroad. Surprisingly, older people and women showed strong migration intent, against the usual stereotype of the young male migrant. The authors urge land-restoration policies that treat staying as a real option.
plos-pone-0353521:
Anan Jarab and seven colleagues check how well heart-attack survivors at an outpatient clinic control their 'bad' cholesterol, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Keeping LDL cholesterol low after a heart attack is one of the surest ways to prevent the next one. A research pharmacist extracted records for two hundred and fifty-five patients and measured their beliefs about medicines and how faithfully they took them.

More than three quarters had uncontrolled LDL — a worrying miss rate. Smoking, uncontrolled blood pressure, and taking beta-blocker medicines each came with higher odds of poor control. The authors argue clinics should pair prescriptions with smoking-cessation help and tighter blood-pressure management rather than simply adding more cholesterol drugs.
plos-pone-0352121:
Heydarpour, Mokhtari, and Dehnavi modeled vaccine supply networks with many products and storage needs in a 2026 study. Vaccines differ in dose schedules and cold demands, from ordinary fridges to ultra-cold freezers. Their math model places distribution centers, assigns vaccines, and sets storage across three tiers, aiming for no shortages at injection sites.

A tailored genetic search solved large cases nearly as well as exact methods that are far slower. Planning many vaccines together, rather than one campaign at a time, matches how real programs run year-round. The model can help health ministries place cold storage where it prevents the most missed vaccinations.
plos-pone-0352321:
Hanji Chen and seven colleagues test a combined therapy for stroke recovery in this 2026 pilot trial. The patients had suffered intracerebral haemorrhage, bleeding inside the brain. Weak legs are a common lasting problem. One group received ear-based vagus nerve stimulation plus repetitive facilitative exercise. The control group got sham stimulation with the same exercise. Sixty patients were split evenly between the arms.

After six weeks, both groups walked and moved better than at the start. Leg function scores, walking category, and stride length all improved. The real-stimulation group improved significantly more on every headline measure. Gait analysis also captured better hip motion in that group. Because the trial was small, the authors frame it as a pilot. The gains justify a larger trial of pairing nerve stimulation with guided exercise.
plos-pone-0352421:
Jiadong Yu, Denitsa Bekerian, and Radhika Khandelwal model why people followed health guidance while information sources fought for their trust. Their 2026 study reanalyses survey data from seven hundred forty-two American adults. During COVID-19, official channels competed with social media and peer networks. The authors traced how each diet of information shaped risk perception, political belief, and conspiracy thinking. Those in turn drove intentions to wear masks and accept vaccination.

Formal sources pushed toward protection. Relying on government sites and mainstream news raised perceived severity and cut conspiracy belief. Both fed stronger protective intentions. Informal sources pulled the other way, softening severity and hardening conspiracies. Perceived severity sat at the model's centre, moving mask use directly and vaccination indirectly. Masking and vaccinating also clustered as one general protective stance. Information strategy, the study implies, is health policy by other means.
plos-pone-0351321:
Sai Sunkara and co-authors stress-tested the electricity grid of the western United States against losing hydropower, which supplies about a quarter of the region's generating capacity. Drought, aging dams, and river rules can all idle hydro plants. The team ran more than sixteen thousand loss scenarios, knocking out hydro across combinations of fourteen river regions, and measured whether the grid could still meet demand.

Some regions punched far above their size: losing their hydro hurt adequacy more than their share of capacity would predict. Losses in paired regions could also compound each other. Tree-based analysis picked out the critical combinations. For grid planners facing a drier West, the study names the basins where backup power, transmission, or water agreements buy the most safety per dollar.
plos-pone-0346421:
Setting ancient Chinese poems to music revives them, but audiences often feel locked out by unfamiliar settings and history. Zushun Zhang, Panjie Xie, and Jinsong Wang studied concerts built around a historic Wei dynasty music score to measure those barriers, in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Borrowing a leisure constraints framework, they built a scale of limiting factors and surveyed audiences at three creative concerts. Barriers fell into three families: personal limits like knowledge and confidence, social limits like companions and guidance, and structural limits like venues and scheduling. The families act in sequence, the analysis showed, so removing later barriers fails while early ones stand.
plos-pone-0351221:
Zhiqiang Yang, Jia Liu, and Qingchao Li turned leftover carbon from coal gas waste into a sponge that pulls an antibiotic from water. Antibiotic traces in rivers harm ecosystems and breed resistance. The team treated the carbon with peroxide to add oxygen rich surface groups, then tested how much trimethoprim, a common antibiotic, it could hold.

Treated carbon held about eighty milligrams per gram, well above the untreated form, and worked well in flowing column tests too. Simulations showed stronger surface attraction and more hydrogen bonds after treatment. A waste product becomes a water cleaner here, though real river trials must still prove cost and safety at scale.
plos-pone-0350221:
Yang Rui and colleagues built a forecasting system for ship paths on inland rivers, with warnings when a ship drifts from its channel. Near river crossing power lines, a drifting ship risks grave harm. Their model stacks time pattern layers, an attention step that weighs speed and heading, and a two way memory unit, trained on real ship tracking data.

Forecast errors fell by roughly a fifth versus strong rival models, and forecast paths hugged real tracks more closely. A layered yaw warning system passed ninety six percent accuracy in typical crossing scenes. River managers could gain earlier, surer warnings to clear ships before they threaten bridges and power lines.
plos-pone-0350821:
Ujin Lee and colleagues studied diet and heart risk in Korean adults. Data came from a national health survey. The years ran from 2016 to 2020. Just over twenty five thousand adults took part. Each adult got a score for a planet friendly diet. That diet favours plants and modest animal foods. Scores were split into four bands.

High scores linked with lower odds of high cholesterol in women. Links also touched belly fat and blood pressure. Some links appeared only in set age groups. No clear links appeared in men. A world diet template may fit Korean food habits unevenly. More work should test the score by sex and age.
plos-pone-0335121:
Emanuela H Kang and colleagues used a computer model of a runner stepping on an obstacle to find safer foot placement for high school cross country athletes. Overuse injuries plague young endurance runners. The model varied joint looseness, foot strike position, and ground friction across twenty seven cases, tracking ligament strain millisecond by millisecond with ground forces and muscle action included.

Foot placement dominated strain. Landing toward the inner foot gave the lowest strain in a key ankle ligament, while centre and outer strikes nearly doubled it. Higher friction lowered strain further. Looser joints raised strain in the foot arch band. Inner placement on grippier ground, the authors advise, is a trainable injury guard.
plos-pone-0344321:
Ginna Patricia Velasco Anacona and colleagues in Colombia studied the genetics of fiber in a wild Andean blueberry in 2026. The fruit, called agraz, is valued for nutrition, but the genes behind its fiber content were almost unknown.

The team measured total, soluble, and insoluble fiber in fruit from many plants, then scanned their DNA for linked spots. They found a set of regions tied to fiber traits, pointing to genes that build and remodel fruit cell walls. One region sat inside a gene from a family that moves sugars. Breeders can use these markers to select plants whose fruit carries more healthy fiber.
plos-pone-0346021:
Habib ur Rehman and two co-authors present new results on fixed points in 2026. A fixed point is a value that a mapping leaves unchanged. Results of this kind help prove that an equation has a solution. They do so even when no formula can produce the solution.

The authors build a four step method for pairs of mappings from a broad class. They prove the steps settle toward a shared fixed point. Worked examples support the proofs. They then apply the method to integral equations in abstract spaces. The scheme gives approximate answers there, not just proof that answers exist.
plos-pone-0347921:
Charlotte Morris, Evangelos Kontopantelis, and co-authors examined who actually receives dementia medicines in English primary care. Drugs called cholinesterase inhibitors, plus memantine, are recommended for Alzheimer's disease and some related dementias. Their 2026 study drew on records from nearly fifteen hundred practices, covering more than two hundred forty thousand patients diagnosed between 2006 and 2024.

Only about six in ten patients ever got one of these medicines, and taking both kinds together stayed rare despite guidelines. People in the poorest areas, some ethnic minority groups, and people with learning disabilities were all less likely to be treated. The authors call the gaps unfair and urge better access, since the pattern suggests need alone is not deciding who gets help.
plos-pone-0350121:
Zoe Sirotiak and Angelique G Brellenthin led talks with adults who live with long COVID. They asked a plain question. Does being active help you, or hurt you? Care teams often urge activity as self-care. But like states can flare with effort. The team held deep talks with thirty-four adults across the United States in 2026.

Near two thirds said activity made them worse. They told of crashes after effort, deep fatigue, and lost skills. A small share, about fifteen in a hundred, felt real gains. They spoke of more energy and a sense of pride. Health scores for the group ran well below US norms. The team says activity plans must fit each person's own limits.
plos-pone-0350021:
Shubham and Rajan Kumar Pandey modeled how tiny nanosheet transistors behave as their parts shrink toward a few nanometers. These transistors are candidates for future computer chips. The study varied gate length and temperature and tracked electron mobility, band gap, and drive current under different kinds of scattering, the collisions that slow electrons inside a device.

Heat hurt performance most: at high temperatures, phonon scattering cut electron mobility by nearly half and slightly narrowed the band gap. Defects at the oxide surface added tunneling paths that waste current. The results map which effects chip designers must control as gates shrink, and where the smallest designs still deliver strong current.
plos-pone-0349621:
Miki Nakamura and colleagues used health checkup records for nearly sixty-five thousand middle-aged adults in Japan's Gunma Prefecture to test how body weight relates to kidney decline. Japan carries one of the world's heaviest dialysis burdens. Checkups from 2018 and 2020 let the team measure whose kidney filtering rate dropped sharply within two years.

The pattern formed a U shape: risk rose at high body mass, as expected with obesity, but also among the underweight, the study's less obvious finding. The analysis accounted for age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, blood sugar, and starting kidney function. Weight advice for kidney protection usually targets heaviness alone; evidence that thinness also carries risk complicates that simple message.
plos-pone-0348221:
Apisith Saraluck and colleagues studied pelvic organ prolapse, the dropping of pelvic organs common after childbirth. They asked which of its features are tied to two bladder problems: trouble emptying and an overactive bladder that creates sudden urgency. Records came from a university hospital clinic in Thailand covering 2018 to 2020. The comparison covered one hundred fifty-one women with emptying difficulty, one hundred thirty-nine with overactive bladder, and a control group with neither.

Most patients were postmenopausal, had given birth more than once, and were overweight. After statistical adjustment, only specific prolapse traits stayed linked to each bladder problem, while many suspected factors fell away. Knowing which prolapse site and severity drive which symptom helps doctors counsel women and choose between watching, exercises, or surgery with better evidence.
plos-pone-0349821:
Pingping Meng and colleagues tested a gene-silencing treatment for the most common kind of hearing loss in mice. Their earlier work showed that a growth factor called neuritin, which supports nerve tissue, falls in the deafened inner ear, and replacing it protected hearing cells. Here they hunted for the tiny RNA switches, microRNAs, that turn neuritin down.

Sequencing the inner ear tissue nominated three microRNAs as the main culprits. Blocking each of them in living mice raised neuritin levels and improved hearing function. With no effective drug yet for sensorineural hearing loss, a treatment that works by releasing a natural protective factor, rather than adding a foreign one, is an appealing direction worth developing.
plos-pone-0348521:
Junghoon Kim and colleagues studied a hidden complication of the ports implanted for chemotherapy in colorectal cancer patients: narrowing of the large vein the port feeds into. Among more than fourteen hundred patients whose first port was placed through the right neck vein between 2015 and 2020, follow-up chest scans showed the narrowing in about one in fifteen.

The team used several statistical methods, including survival analysis and a decision-tree method, to find which traits raised the risk. They also checked whether two common cancer drugs changed the odds in patients receiving palliative care. A narrowed vein can swell the arm and complicate treatment, so knowing who is at risk helps doctors choose port sites and watch the right patients with scans.
plos-pone-0349221:
Kayoko Ito and co-workers follow what shapes saliva flow and the feeling of a dry mouth in healthy young men. Dry mouth can occur even when saliva output looks normal, which makes it tricky to judge. Their 2026 study repeats measures over time in thirty-nine men, tracking room heat and moisture, body water loss, and stress markers in saliva.

Resting saliva flow moved with room temperature, humidity, hydration, and one stress marker. Flow during chewing showed no such links. The dry-mouth feeling itself tied only to one stress marker. Because room conditions shift with the seasons, clinics measuring saliva need to record them. The work also hints that stress plays a quiet part in dry-mouth complaints.
plos-pone-0347321:
JungHo Jo and co-workers lay out a trial plan for Chuna, a Korean hands-on therapy, in people with longer-lasting low back pain. Chuna treatment is guided by X-ray readings of how the spine sits. Their 2026 protocol describes a randomized trial at two hospitals with forty-six patients whose pain has lasted at least three weeks.

Half will get usual care plus Chuna sessions twice a week for four weeks, shaped to each person's X-ray pattern. The other half will get usual care alone. Pain and daily function will be tracked to three months, along with safety. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it sets up the first rigorous test of X-ray-guided Chuna care.
plos-pone-0349021:
Mingfei Li and Shanshan Huang map what researchers know about anxiety felt by consumers while shopping and spending. Worry tied to buying seems to be rising with climate fears, money strain, and rapid tech change. Their 2026 review gathers sixty articles from major databases and sorts out what sparks such anxiety, what it leads to, and where it sits between the two.

Studies link consumer anxiety to choices, well-being, and buying behavior in many settings, but the work remains scattered. Gaps include how anxiety plays out over time and across cultures. The authors lay out a shared framework and a research agenda. Shops and brands also get practical hints for calming worried customers instead of exploiting them.
plos-pone-0348021:
Hannah Linney, Ken van Someren, and Sinead Keogh lay out a plan to review research on teenagers' skill at judging health information online. Teens form habits that last into adulthood while swimming in digital health claims, some of them false. Their 2026 protocol describes a scoping review across five databases, screening studies of young people's ability to find, judge, and use online health content.

The review will sort what kinds of studies exist, where they were done, and which skills they measured. Screening follows a standard reporting checklist, with a second reviewer checking part of the records. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. The finished map should show schools and health services where teen digital health skills are least understood.
plos-pone-0345521:
Berta Munne-Barellas and her team sat down with health staff in Catalonia, Spain. Twenty-one staff took part, from GPs and nurses to birth pros. The talks dug into a hard spot in their work: drugs, shots, and herb cures for women with child or at the breast. Proof is thin there, and rules urge great care.

Each trade met its own snags. GPs and nurses felt short on birth care drills. Birth pros prized close watch when drugs must change. Womb pros feared that some women now shun drugs they need. Flu and cough shots won trust, while the COVID shot still drew doubt. The team backs shared calls and more drills.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 221 is a UN Security Council enforcement step against Rhodesia's oil lifeline, adopted on 9 April 1966 by ten votes to none with five abstentions. After the white minority regime's unilateral independence declaration, oil tankers were heading for Beira in Portuguese Mozambique, from where a pipeline could pump fuel to landlocked Southern Rhodesia.

The Council declares the situation a threat to the peace, calls on Portugal not to allow pumping or accept Rhodesian oil at Beira, and asks all states to divert their suspect vessels. Most strikingly, it authorizes Britain to use force if necessary to stop such ships, and specifically to arrest the tanker Joanna V if her cargo were discharged. The episode became known as the Beira Patrol.

Sierra Leone's battered UN mission gained a short lifeline in 2000. On 20 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1321. The force, UNAMSIL, had been built in 1999 to back a peace deal. That spring, rebels had seized hundreds of its peacekeepers as hostages. Fresh troops and reviews had followed in August and early September.

Three short lines do the work here. The mandate runs to 31 December 2000. The Council will review the state of play by the end of October. It stays seized of the matter in the meantime. The bridge carried the mission toward its stronger form of 2001. That form finally broke the rebels' grip on the country.

Yugoslavia was tearing itself apart in late November 1991. A ceasefire signed in Geneva on 23 November offered brief hope. The Secretary-General's envoy, Cyrus Vance, had brokered it. Yugoslav leaders told him they wanted UN peacekeepers deployed quickly. Resolution 721 gave the Council's answer that month.

Members approved the envoy's peace efforts warmly. They endorsed his warning to the parties. No peacekeeping force could deploy without full respect for the Geneva deal. The Yugoslav sides were urged to honor it completely. The Council promised to act fast on any peacekeeping proposal. That promise led, within months, to the huge UNPROFOR mission in Croatia and Bosnia.

Summer 2008 brought the Golan force to the table once more. The chief's report of 16 June 2008 told of a calm line. UNDOF's term was set to lapse at the month's end. The force had stood on the heights since 1974. Resolution 1821 passed on 27 June 2008.

Six more months were set, to 31 December 2008. Both sides heard the old call to act on the 1973 text. The staff code clause runs long in this text. Zero tolerance for sexual abuse is the theme. Troop states must drill their men, probe claims, and punish guilt. A report was due when the term closed. The twin frame of these late texts is plain: still guns on the line, strict rules for the watch.

Senegal's charge against Portugal wins backing in Resolution 321. It passed on 23 October 1972, with twelve votes in favor and three members not voting either way. Senegal's foreign chief laid out the case in the hall. Portugal replied by letter. Past texts since 1963 had dealt with Portuguese strikes on Senegalese soil. The strikes came from the colony of Guinea-Bissau, next door. A UN rights team's report of 1971 set out the facts in depth.

The Council voiced deep dismay at Portugal's flat refusal to obey those texts. It condemned the strikes and told Lisbon to respect Senegal's soil and borders. Calm would come, it argued, when all African lands near Portugal's colonies were left in peace, and their peoples freed to rule their own fate.

Resolution 1621, adopted on 6 September 2005, reinforces the UN mission in Congo ahead of historic elections. The Pretoria transition agreement of 2002 was moving the country toward its first free national polls in four decades. The Council called on the transitional institutions and all Congolese parties to keep the elections free, fair, and peaceful, and to respect the electoral commission's timetable exactly.

To guard the process, the Council authorized a temporary increase in the strength of MONUC, the UN mission, which already operated under Chapter VII. Donors funding the election effort were thanked and pressed to keep giving. The text also records continuing alarm at hostilities in the east and at attacks on civilians by armed groups.

South Africa's arms buildup is the subject of Resolution 421, adopted on 9 December 1977. A month earlier, in Resolution 418, the Council had ruled that South Africa getting arms threatened world peace and had placed a required arms embargo on the country. Members now wanted a way to watch how well that ban was working.

The resolution creates a Security Council committee made up of all Council members. The committee must study the Secretary-General's report on the embargo, look for ways to make the ban work better, and ask states what they have done to enforce it. All states are called on to cooperate and share information, and the Secretary-General must give the committee the staff and help it needs.

Resolution 1921, adopted on 12 May 2010, extends the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, one more time while setting its exit. The deadline for Nepal's new constitution was 28 May 2010, yet the parties had reached no agreement on the text or on extending the Constituent Assembly. Discharge of disqualified Maoist army personnel, including minors, had been completed under a December 2009 action plan. Nepal asked for UNMIN to stay until 15 September 2010.

The Council renews UNMIN until 15 September 2010. It decides that UNMIN should start arranging its withdrawal at once, handing over leftover monitoring duties by that date. It calls on the government and the Maoist party to agree on a timed plan, with clear targets, for integrating and settling Maoist army personnel. A report on carrying out the resolution is due by 1 September 2010.

Côte d'Ivoire's transition is extended one final year under African Union terms in Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections had proved impossible on schedule. The transition and the mandates of the president and prime minister expired on 31 October 2006. The AU Peace and Security Council had set new terms on 17 October 2006.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the AU decision. The president remains head of state for a final transition of no more than twelve months. The prime minister's mandate is renewed on the same terms, barred from standing in the coming election. The prime minister receives powers including rule by ordinance and authority over the defence and security forces, to deliver disarmament, voter identification, and elections by 31 October 2007. The High Representative for the Elections is renewed for twelve months as arbitrator of electoral disputes and certifier of all stages.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution ES-10/21 was adopted by the General Assembly at its tenth emergency special session in October 2023. Its title is Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations. It answered the sharp rise in violence from 7 October 2023 and the fast worsening crisis in the Gaza Strip and the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory.

The Assembly called for an immediate, durable, and lasting humanitarian truce leading to an end to the fighting. It demanded full respect for the laws of war. It demanded steady delivery of water, food, medicine, fuel, and power to civilians in Gaza. It also demanded access for aid agencies and the release of civilians held captive. It demanded no forced transfer of the Palestinian population.

The General Assembly adopted Resolution 21 on 10 February 1946, at the twenty-eighth plenary meeting. It arranged the first meeting of the International Court of Justice. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to call the Court together at The Hague as soon as its judges were elected. He was to name a temporary secretary and staff. He was to open talks with the Carnegie Foundation on the terms for the Court's use of rooms in the Peace Palace.

General Assembly resolution 69/21 (2014) concerns the Division for Palestinian Rights of the Secretariat, the office that supports the Assembly's Palestinian rights committee. The Assembly judges the Division's work useful and helpful and asks the Secretary-General to keep funding it. Its tasks include watching developments and holding international meetings. They include running the 'Question of Palestine' website and its information system, and publishing materials. They include training Palestinian government staff. They include holding the annual exhibit for the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People on 29 November.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 121 was adopted unanimously on 12 December 1956. It recommends to the General Assembly that Japan be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Council had examined Japan's application. Its file before the Council included documents from 1952 and from the autumn of 1956. Acting on a membership application is one of the few steps the Charter reserves to the Council and the Assembly together. No state can join the United Nations without a Council recommendation first.

Two lines are all this bridge measure needs. On 3 July 2002, acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the provisions of its resolution 1357 of 2001, on the former Yugoslavia, would stay in force until 15 July 2002. The matter stayed under review while the follow-on arrangements covered by that earlier text were settled.

Liberia's sanctions regime is rebuilt from the ground up on 22 December 2003, after its civil war. Expert panels had found the old measures still being breached, mainly through arms buying. A peace agreement had been signed in Accra in August, and a transitional government had taken office in October.

The old prohibitions are ended and the old sanctions committee dissolved, then a fresh set of measures is imposed under a new committee. These cover arms, rough diamonds from Liberia, and timber, matched to the new situation on the ground. West African states are told to stop armed groups from using their territory to attack neighbours, and reviews are set to test whether the transitional government meets the Council's conditions.

Pacific islands once held by Japan came before the Council on 2 April 1947. The islands had been German colonies before the First World War. The League of Nations then gave them to Japan as a mandate. Japan lost them in the Second World War. Resolution 21, adopted unanimously, set up a trusteeship for the islands.

The Council approved the terms of the trusteeship and made the United States the administering authority. The islands were classed as a strategic area. Because of that, the United States could build bases and station forces there. In return, it had to move the islanders toward self-government. It had to protect their lands and rights. It also had to build up education, health services, and the local economy.
un-ga-res-es-10-21:
The General Assembly, not the Security Council, adopted Resolution ES-10/21 in October 2023. It came at the Assembly's tenth emergency special session. The war in Gaza had begun after the attack of 7 October 2023. The Assembly voiced grave concern at the worsening situation in the occupied Palestinian territory.

The resolution condemned all violence against Palestinian and Israeli civilians. It called for an immediate, durable, and sustained humanitarian truce, leading to a halt to the fighting. All parties were told to obey international humanitarian and human rights law. Civilians and civilian objects had to be protected. Aid, supplies, and basic services had to reach everyone in need in the Gaza Strip. The text also restated the duty to respect the Geneva Conventions in all circumstances. Because it is an Assembly text, its call carried political weight rather than binding orders.
un-sc-res-221:
Oil tankers bound for Beira, with fuel for Rhodesia's illegal regime, drew a rare call to action at sea on 9 April 1966. One tanker had already arrived at Beira, in Portuguese Mozambique. Another was on its way. A pipeline ran from Beira to Southern Rhodesia. The Council had already ordered states to cut the regime off from oil. Resolution 221 answers those reports.

The Council decided that the situation was a threat to the peace. Portugal was told not to let oil be pumped through the pipeline to Rhodesia, nor to accept oil at Beira meant for Rhodesia. All states had to divert any of their own ships believed to be carrying such oil. Britain was called on to stop suspect tankers from reaching Beira, by force if needed. It could arrest and hold the tanker named in the text after unloading.
un-sc-res-1321:
Sierra Leone's peace remained fragile in the autumn of 2000. On 20 September 2000 the Security Council extended its mission there, UNAMSIL. The new term ran until 31 December 2000. The Council also set a deadline for itself. It would review the situation again no later than 31 October. Earlier resolutions had built the mission up after rebels seized peacekeepers that spring.

The short extension kept United Nations troops in place through the year-end. It bought time to judge whether the ceasefire could hold. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. Sierra Leone's war, fought over government control and diamonds, still had more than a year to run.
un-sc-res-721:
Fighting in Yugoslavia deepened in the autumn of 1991. The parties had signed a ceasefire deal in Geneva on 23 November. The Secretary-General's personal envoy had carried that agreement to the Council. On 27 November 1991 the Council backed his warning to the parties. A peacekeeping operation, he had said, could not be deployed without full respect for the Geneva deal.

The Council also restated its arms embargo from resolution 713. It deplored the heavy loss of life and wide damage in the fighting. Neighboring states felt the effects as well. The Council stayed seized of the matter until a peaceful solution came. The envoy's warning framed the mission that followed months later.
un-sc-res-1821:
The Golan Heights force closed out 2008 with a routine renewal. On 27 June 2008 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2008. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The Council welcomed the force's work on staff conduct rules. UNDOF enforced the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its members had to meet the United Nations code of conduct in full.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. A closing report was due at the term's end. It would cover events and steps taken toward 338. UNDOF's patrols kept the separation zone quiet. That calm had held, with rare breaks, since the force arrived in 1974.
un-sc-res-321:
Portugal's attack on a Senegalese border post was condemned on 23 October 1972. Senegal's complaint told of regular Portuguese troops striking the post at Nianao on 12 October 1972. Earlier Council texts, from 178 (1963) to 302 (1971), had condemned Portuguese violence in Senegal again and again. Lisbon refused to comply with any of them. Incidents along the borders of Guinea-Bissau, Angola, and Mozambique kept growing.

The Council condemned the frontier violation and the attack on Nianao. It recalled resolution 294 (1971) on Portuguese acts of violence and destruction. Portugal was told to stop at once, and for good, every act of violence and destruction against Senegal. Lisbon also had to respect self-determination and independence for the peoples of its territories, as the 1960 declaration set out. The Council declared that if Portugal failed to comply, it would meet to weigh other steps.
un-sc-res-1621:
MONUC gained election reinforcements on 6 September 2005. Congo's transition rested on the Global and All Inclusive Agreement signed at Pretoria in 2002. Elections were the base for lasting peace and the rule of law, the Council stressed. Transitional bodies had to hold free, fair, and peaceful polls and keep the electoral commission's timetable. Armed groups in the east still threatened the vote.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council approved the Secretary-General's recommendations and concept of operations for the elections. It authorized a temporary rise in MONUC's strength of 841 personnel, soldiers and police, to help secure the polls. The extra deployment would end by 1 July 2006 at the latest, and its short-term character was underlined. MONUC was encouraged, within its means, to give the electoral process its full support. The Council stayed actively seized. The boost covered the run-up to polling day.
un-sc-res-421:
South Africa's mandatory arms embargo gained its watchdog on 9 December 1977. Resolution 418 (1977), passed that November, had judged South Africa's arms build-up a threat to the peace. It banned arms sales to Pretoria under Chapter VII. The Council now judged that the ban needed machinery to check its progress. The Secretary-General already owed a report on the embargo's working.

The Council set up a committee of all its members under rule 28 of its rules. The committee would examine the Secretary-General's report on the embargo. It would study ways to make the mandatory ban bite harder and advise the Council. It would seek from every state fresh word on the steps taken to apply resolution 418. All states were called to cooperate with the committee in full and supply the facts it sought. The Secretary-General had to give the committee every help it needed.
un-sc-res-1921:
Nepal is the subject of Resolution 1921 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 12 May 2010. A ten-year civil war had ended there in 2006. The United Nations Mission in Nepal, called UNMIN, watched over arms and fighters after the war.

The text renews the mission's mandate until 15 September 2010, at the Nepali government's request. It notes worry that parties had not yet agreed on a new constitution. It calls on the government and the Maoists to set a clear plan for former fighters. The mission was told to prepare its withdrawal by the same date.
un-sc-res-1721:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections could not be held on time, and the transition period had expired the day before. The African Union had ruled on how the country should be run until a vote was possible. The crisis kept causing large-scale suffering and displacement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs the African Union plan in full. The president stays as head of state for one final transition of at most twelve months. The prime minister also stays, barred from running in the coming election. He gains full powers to deliver the road map, including command over the security forces. Elections must happen by 31 October 2007.
europmc-pmc10203321:
Yang and colleagues review epigenetic regulation in the tumor microenvironment in a 2023 paper. Epigenetics covers changes that switch genes on or off without altering the DNA code itself. Such switches, from chemical marks on DNA and histones to reshaped packaging and RNA changes, help control how cancers start and grow.

The review explains how these switches act not just in tumor cells but in the immune and support cells around them. It shows how they shape response to immune therapy. It also surveys drugs that reset faulty switches, a growing front in cancer care.
europmc-pmc10480221:
Xie and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how drug hunters now chase proteins once deemed undruggable. Such proteins have shapes or jobs that defy the usual drug design playbook. Their size and smooth surfaces leave no snug pocket for a drug to grip. Yet many drive major diseases, so the prize for success is large.

Fresh tactics fill the review by Xie. Some drugs bind for good to a target, while others grip a side pocket to shut it down. Other routes break the protein, silence its gene, or block its talks with partners. RNA-based drugs and immune therapy add more angles. The team tracks which of these have reached patient trials.
europmc-pmc10484921:
Leguia and colleagues traced a bird flu strain in Peru in 2023 as it killed sea life in bulk. The strain is H5N1, a highly harmful form of avian flu. It reached Peru in November 2022 and sparked huge die-offs of pelicans and sea lions. The team read the virus genome from five kinds of wild animal.

Samples came from dolphins, sea lions, sanderlings, pelicans, and cormorants. The Peru viruses mixed parts from two lines, one from Eurasia and one from North America. Four genome parts came from each line, Leguia reports. The viruses were also gaining changes fast, some of concern. The team urges close local watch to curb spread to other species, humans included.
europmc-pmc10515021:
Sun, Rao, Zhou, and Li reviewed plant carotenoids in 2022, the pigments that colour many fruits and leaves. Plants make these compounds from scratch in light-using tissues. In plants they aid light capture, guard against light harm, and give colour to petals and fruit. They also feed into plant hormones and signals.

For humans, carotenoids are the raw stock for vitamin A. Sun notes that they also act as antioxidants in the diet, soaking up cell-damaging bits. New regulators of their build-up keep turning up in lab work. The review sums up how plants control their levels at many steps. Farm uses include richer crops with more of these healthy pigments.
europmc-pmc10564921:
Clusmann and co-authors mapped the future of large language models in medicine in 2023. Such models are AI tools trained to write and process text. ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 drew world notice. The models can answer, sum up, and translate text at near-human level.

That skill tempts clinics, schools, and labs, Clusmann notes. Wider access to medical facts could help patients and staff. The same tools could spread false claims just as fast. Weak openness about how they work adds risk for fraud and error. The review sorts gains and caps for care, research, and teaching. It urges clear rules on blame when a model errs.
europmc-pmc11080421:
Rahimi and Khatooni clarify a key quality concept in interview-based nursing research in this 2024 paper. Saturation is the point where new interviews stop adding fresh insight. Judging it well is essential for rigorous qualitative research, meaning research based on words rather than numbers. The authors used an evolutionary concept analysis, a method that traces how a concept's meaning shifts over time.

They analysed 33 articles and books from 2005 to 2023. Saturation proved to be context-dependent and subjective, needing detailed systematic work, they found. It is used in four senses: theoretical, data, code or theme, and meaning saturation. Causes split into study factors and researcher factors. Reaching it secures credibility and quality while saving time, energy, and budget. Two independent researchers checked the analysis for validity.
europmc-pmc11121021:
GBD 2021 Forecasting Collaborators project disease burden to 2050 for 204 countries and territories in this 2024 analysis. Policy makers need future trends in disease and its drivers to plan long-term health spending. The team built a reference forecast, meaning the most likely future, plus what-if scenarios. Those scenarios ask what changes if chosen risk factors were eliminated by 2050.

Forecasts cover deaths, years of life lost, years lived with disability, and a combined measure, split by age and sex. Drivers include a socio-demographic index built from income, schooling, and fertility. Only risk factors judged causal in the parent study shape each cause's path. Results are given for 21 regions, seven super-regions, and the world. The work expands earlier Global Burden of Disease forecasts with improved methods.
europmc-pmc11392821:
Dimitrov and colleagues present an all-in-one framework for inferring cell-to-cell communication in this 2024 paper. Cells signal to each other, and new methods read gene activity in single cells or in tissue spots to guess those signals. Each past tool caught only part of the picture. The team set out to unify them.

Their framework, LIANA+, rests on a rich base of known signal pairs. It works on single-cell data and on spatial data, where each spot on a tissue slice is read in place. It also handles data that mixes several conditions or several measurement types at once. Rather than replace past methods, it extends and unifies them, the authors say. The code is shared openly, with many worked examples. They present it as a scalable answer for decoding signals within and between cells.
europmc-pmc11802921:
Zheng and co-authors published a 2025 review on the most common form of liver cancer. That form is called hepatocellular carcinoma, or HCC for short. It makes up about nine in ten liver cancer cases. The review links it to hepatitis B and C, to a food toxin, and to metabolic disease.

Readers get a map of the cell signals that drive growth, spread, and return of these tumors. Some signals guide cell growth, while others shape cell identity and stress response. Zheng also surveys drugs that block those signals. The work helps doctors match treatments to tumor biology.
europmc-pmc11889221:
Guan and co-authors reviewed tissue macrophages in a 2025 survey. Macrophages are immune cells that patrol tissues across the body. They eat dead cells and germs, and they present alarms to other cells. They also help repair damage and keep tissues in balance.

Origins vary more than once thought, and the review sorts them out. Some macrophages arise early in development, others from blood stem cells. In tumors they can help or hinder cancer growth. Guan links their states to heart, immune, and cancer disease. That link makes them targets for new drugs.
europmc-pmc1257421:
van der Helm-van Mil and colleagues compared two forms of rheumatoid arthritis in 2005. Antibodies to citrullinated proteins mark one form of the disease. They appear before symptoms and are highly specific. Genetic risks differ between antibody-positive and antibody-negative patients.

The cohort held 454 new patients, split near evenly by antibody status. Early symptoms and joint counts were recorded at entry. Blood inflammation levels were also compared. Disease course over time was tracked for both groups. The study tests whether the two forms behave as distinct diseases. Separate mechanisms would call for separate care logic.
europmc-pmc1334221:
Parikh and co-authors linked a vessel protein to lung leak in sepsis in 2006. Sepsis can trigger acute respiratory distress syndrome, a deadly lung failure. Vessel leak drives that failure, but its mediators were unclear. Angiopoietin-2 blocks a vessel-stabilizing receptor and was the suspect.

Blood levels of angiopoietin-2 ran significantly higher in sepsis patients. The elevation was clearest in patients with impaired oxygenation. Serum from those patients disrupted vessel cell architecture in dishes. Mouse and cell studies backed the human pattern. Parikh names angiopoietin-2 as a contributor to septic leak.
europmc-pmc1665421:
Lead harms the developing mind most at a specific stage of pregnancy. Hu and co-authors pinpointed that stage in 2006, following 146 pregnant women in Mexico City. They measured lead in blood and plasma each trimester, then tested the children at 12 and 24 months.

Only first-trimester lead predicted lower mental development scores. A one standard deviation rise in first-trimester plasma lead cost 3.5 points on the index. Later pregnancy lead, and the child's own later blood lead, mattered less. Plasma lead, the fraction that can cross to the fetus, beat whole blood lead as a predictor. Hu urges prevention aimed at early pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1831521: Exposure of perfluorinated chemicals through lactation: levels of matched human milk and serum and a temporal trend, 1996-2004, in Sweden. — a 2005 science paper on PFCs in breast milk. It measures the milk levels. The paper is the PFC-milk study: the findings on perfluorinated ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2072821: Polyfluoroalkyl chemicals in the U.S. population: data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2003-2004 and comparisons with NHANES — a 2005 science paper on polyfluoroalkyl levels. It tracks the chemical levels. The paper is the level study: the findings on NHANES, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2267221: A systematic assessment of MHC class II peptide binding predictions and evaluation of a consensus approach. — a 2005 science paper on immune-tag match math. It grades the tag-match math for labs. The paper is the match-grade study: the notes on immune ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2275221: Dynamics and evolution of the inverted repeat-large single copy junctions in the chloroplast genomes of monocots. — a 2005 science paper on chloroplast junction shifts. It tracks the junction dynamics. The paper is the junction study: the findings on monocots, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2292821: Interleukin-23 restrains regulatory T cell activity to drive T cell-dependent colitis. — a 2005 science paper on IL-23 and colitis. It finds the IL-23 restraint. The paper is the restraint study: the findings on colitis, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2323621: Isolation of a strong Arabidopsis guard cell promoter and its potential as a research tool. — a 2008 science paper on a guard-cell promoter. It isolates the strong promoter. The paper is the promoter study: the findings on Arabidopsis, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2327221: Hypoglycaemia in Type 2 diabetes. — a 2008 science paper on low blood sugar in diabetes. It reviews the low-sugar ills for labs. The paper is the low-sugar review: the notes on diabetes, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2375021: The DAVID Gene Functional Classification Tool: a novel biological module-centric algorithm to f — a 2008 science paper on the DAVID classification tool. It guides the classification tool. The paper is the DAVID guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2440421: Systemic complement activation in age-related macular degeneration. — a 2008 science paper on body-wide eye-attack ills. It spots the body-wide attack for labs. The paper is the attack study: the notes on eye ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2518121: Drug-selected human lung cancer stem cells: cytokine network, tumorigenic and metastatic proper — a 2008 science paper on drug-selected lung stem cells. It studies the cytokine network. The paper is the network study: the findings on lung ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2602721: Root System Architecture from Coupling Cell Shape to Auxin Transport — a 2008 science paper on root system architecture. It couples the cell shape. The paper is the root study: the findings on auxin ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2637921: Tuberculosis drug resistance mutation database. — a 2008 science paper on the TB drug-shield list. It lists the drug shields for labs. The paper is the shield list: the notes on TB ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2646321: Association between administered oxygen, arterial partial oxygen pressure and mortality in mech — a 2008 science paper on oxygen and mortality. It links the administered oxygen. The paper is the link study: the findings on oxygen ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2722021: Genomic and transcriptional co-localization of protein-coding and long non-coding RNA pairs in — a 2008 science paper on genomic co-localization. It maps the transcriptional pairs. The paper is the mapping study: the findings on genome ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2746121: Automated MAD and MIR structure solution. — a 2008 science paper on auto-shape solvers. It solves the auto shapes for labs. The paper is the solver study: the findings on shape ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
aratus-phaenomena-mair-1921:
A. W. Mair translated Aratus's Phaenomena for the Loeb series in 1921. The volume adds works by Callimachus and Lycophron beside Aratus. Aratus composed his astronomical poem around 275 BCE at a Macedonian court.

The Phaenomena maps the constellations in elegant Greek verse. Weather signs drawn from animals, winds, and the moon fill its second half. Farmers and sailors used the poem as a practical almanac. It became the most-read poem of antiquity after Homer, roughly speaking. Saint Paul even quotes a line from Aratus in the New Testament. Mair's Loeb gives Greek facing English throughout the volume. Science as poetry describes the Phaenomena's lasting appeal.
oe-physiologus-cook-1921:
The Old English Physiologus survives only as a fragment, three beast poems in Anglo-Saxon verse. Albert Cook edited what remains in 1921, with modern English translations beside the old text. The Panther, the Whale, and a lost Partridge piece are all that time has left of the English version.

The Panther's sweet breath draws all beasts, a figure of Christ drawing the world. The Whale tricks sailors who camp on its back, a warning against the devil's false ground. Each poem joins close description to moral meaning. Cook's edition presents text, translation, and notes together. Three beasts and three morals survive, in the tongue of Beowulf's scribes.
fontenelle-histoire-des-oracles-french-1:
Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle, the French man of letters, wrote his Histoire des oracles from the learning of the Dutch scholar Van Dale. This edition of 1721 kept the work before French readers. Fontenelle treats the pagan oracles of Greece and Rome, once thought to speak with the voices of gods or demons.

His verdict is elegant and deadly. The oracles were priestly frauds, kept up for profit and power, and they faded when politics changed. Wit does the work of demolition in graceful French prose. The book became the Enlightenment's classic doubting account of pagan divination. Oracles, one might say, were laughed out of court by the politest executioner in Paris.
prierias-de-strigimagarum-latin-1521:
Silvestro Mazzolini, called Prierias, was the papal theologian who first answered Luther in print. His three Latin books on the marvels of witches and demons appeared in 1521. The work is the first Dominican demonology after the Malleus Maleficarum, and it carried huge influence at the papal court.

Prierias defends the reality of witches' deeds against the old skeptical canon. His learning marshals Scripture, law, and reported cases in scholastic ranks. Rome's theologian here lends the hammer his weight. The book shows the Vatican's own scholar building doctrine for the hunts. Students of the Malleus tradition read Prierias as its first great reinforcement from the top of the church.
plos-pone-0004921:
A crawling cell pushes out a flat sheet called a lamellipod. The sheet is a web of actin protein. That web is constantly torn down and rebuilt. Takahiro Tsuji and colleagues timed two rival parts of this turnover. They used single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. One part is new web growth by the Arp2/3 complex. The other is web breaking by a protein named AIP1.

AIP1-linked disruption ran about ten times faster than Arp2/3 nucleation. The tearing-down side of the cycle is far quicker than assumed. The result helps settle a debate about how the cell's crawling edge renews itself.
plos-pone-0005021:
Cell division ends with two cells pinching apart. A bridge called the midbody manages the final steps. The midbody had been described only in animals. Laura Eme and colleagues traced its parts across the tree of life. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Other eukaryotes use varied structures for the same final steps.

The team found the midbody's protein machinery is ancient. A complex division apparatus existed in the last common ancestor of eukaryotes. Fungi and plants remodeled that inheritance in their own ways. Cell division's toolkit is far older than assumed. The finding pushes a complex structure back over a billion years.
plos-pone-0005121:
Fins and limbs share ancient blueprints. Small timing changes reshape them during evolution. Koji Sakamoto and colleagues found one such change in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared gene expression during fin development. Their focus was Sonic hedgehog, a key patterning signal. Hox genes control when it switches on.

A heterochronic shift moved the signal's timing. Heterochronic means a change in developmental timing. The shift in Hox-mediated activation led to morphological changes in the fin. Timing is the sculptor here. Evolution remodels bodies by resetting developmental clocks. The work shows that process at the gene level. It connects two famous gene families in one mechanism.
plos-pone-0005221:
Brucellosis is among the most widespread diseases passed from animals to people. Animals are almost the only source of human infection, so testing cattle quickly matters. Bronsvoort and colleagues compared a fast flow test for brucellosis antibodies with the standard lab test in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The work was done in West African zebu cattle, the Bos indicus breed common in the region. The reference test, called cELISA, is accurate but needs a proper lab. A field-ready test that matches it would let vets screen herds on the spot and act sooner.
plos-pone-0005321:
