Newborn screening uses dried blood spots to catch metabolic diseases early. The same spots could screen for immune disorders, which number more than a hundred. Janzi and colleagues tested microarray screening for one such disorder, C3 deficiency, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

C3 is a core protein of the complement system, part of early immune defense. Babies missing it face severe infections before anyone suspects an immune fault. A blood-spot microarray test could add immune screening to the panel every newborn already receives. One more test on the same drop of blood costs a lab very little. So a screen that rides on the blood spots already drawn from each newborn is an easy win for child health.
plos-pone-0005921:
Random ups and downs in protein levels are a fact of cell life. Anatoly Mayburd asked in 2009 whether that noise could help start long-term disease. His PLOS ONE paper argues that chance shifts in gene expression, seen first in nerve precursor cells, may push cells toward a sick state over time.

Mayburd links the same noise to how treatment might work. If random change can tip a cell into disease, then therapy may need to calm the noise, not just fix one gene. The paper offers a frame for thinking about chronic illness that starts from chance events inside cells rather than from clear outside causes.
plos-pone-0006021:
A memory may be stored one tiny spine at a time. Amadou Corera, Guy Doucet and Edward Fon tested that scale of learning in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies long-term potentiation, the lasting boost a synapse gains after strong use, inside single dendritic spines cut off from the rest of the neuron.

Even in isolation, a spine could gain that lasting boost, the title reports. The change runs through NMDA receptors and a rise in AMPA receptors, the standard machinery of this kind of learning. Showing that one spine alone can learn makes the spine the smallest known stage for memory, a fact that guides models of how brains store experience.
plos-pone-0006121:
Schizophrenia disables about one person in a hundred, and its causes run partly in the genes. Jinong Feng, Guihua Sun, Jin Yan and colleagues looked for clues on the X chromosome in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper gathers evidence tying schizophrenia to alterations in microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, including parts of the machinery that processes them, which earlier work had linked to X-linked intellectual disability.

An X-chromosome pattern would help explain the disease's uneven run through families and sexes. MicroRNAs each tune many genes at once, so a few altered ones can bend brain development broadly. The evidence assembled here gives genetics a defined place to dig next in a disease that has resisted simple answers.
plos-pone-0006221:
A gut hormone called GLP-1 helps pancreatic beta cells release insulin when sugar rises. Marie-Line Peyot and colleagues asked whether its signals also steer how beta cells burn fuel, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of rodent cells. GLP-1 and a related drug switch on several known signal pathways in these cells.

The title states the conclusion: those signals do not drive fuel and energy metabolism in the cells. Insulin release and energy burning appear to be run by separate controls. The distinction matters for diabetes drugs based on GLP-1. Sharper mechanism maps help drug makers predict benefits and side effects more accurately.
plos-pone-0006721:
Anne-Cécile Huby and co-authors studied kidney damage in mice engineered to overproduce renin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protein leaking into urine marks declining kidney function. It also predicts heart disease risk. The leak is tied to broken slit diaphragms and lost podocyte foot processes. Those structural changes were long considered irreversible.

Podocytes are the cells that wrap kidney filters. The transgenic mice overexpressing renin develop chronic renal disease. The authors examined whether podocyte structure could be restored. They also tracked whether kidney disease improved along with structure. Evidence of repair would challenge the idea that this damage is permanent. It would open new options for treating chronic kidney disease.
plos-pone-0006821:
Clarence C. Gravlee, Amy L. Non, and Connie J. Mulligan studied blood pressure, ancestry, and race in southeastern Puerto Rico in PLOS ONE in 2009. Race in genetics and medicine is a contested topic. Debates weigh genetic against sociocultural explanations for health gaps. Few studies integrate both kinds of evidence. The authors set out to combine them in one population.

They measured genetic ancestry alongside social classification of race. Then they related both to blood pressure inequalities. The design asks whether genes or social labels track health better. Results speak to how medicine should use race at all. The study is a model for separating ancestry from social experience.
plos-pone-0006921:
Laith Yakob and Guiyun Yan published a modelling study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on malaria control. Their subject was integrated vector management, an approach drawing fresh interest at the time. They asked what happens when two tools are combined instead of used alone. The tools were larval habitat source reduction and insecticide-treated bed nets.

The model attacks several points in the malaria transmission cycle at once. Yakob and Yan reasoned that combined pressure might act together and beat single-tool programs. Bed nets alone were then the main intervention in wide use. Their work gives malaria planners a way to test combined strategies before field trials.
plos-pone-0007021:
Joseph Jeffry, Shuang-Quan Yu, Parul Sikand, and colleagues targeted pain fibers in the spinal cord in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic pain is a major clinical problem. Opiates are often the only treatment, yet they bring sedation and dangerous breathing suppression. The team focused on sensory terminals carrying the receptor TRPV1.

They used resiniferatoxin, a powerful TRPV1 activator, delivered to the spinal cord. Silencing just those nerve endings promised pain relief without whole-body drug effects. Long lasting analgesia from one targeted treatment would be a real advance. It could spare patients the daily risks of opioid therapy.
plos-pone-0007121:
Dru Dace, Aslam Khan, Jennifer Stark, and colleagues studied a nerve disease driven by immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Demyelinating polyneuropathy strips insulation from nerves. It comes in acute form as Guillain-Barré syndrome, and in chronic forms too. Interleukin-10 is usually classed as an anti-inflammatory signal. Yet it had also been tied to abnormal immune activity.

The team raised IL-10 levels and watched the disease that followed. Excess IL-10 promoted a chronic, macrophage-driven nerve damage. The damage depended on the Fas ligand death pathway. The result warns that a calming signal can harm in the wrong setting.
plos-pone-0007221:
Wayne Dawson and Kenji Yamamoto considered schooling during a fast-spreading epidemic in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Large cities move people quickly through transport networks. An airborne or contact pathogen can ride those routes and spread through a whole population in a short time.

The authors argue that home education may fare best in the right social setting. They point to extended family culture and an aging society as helpful conditions. Their model links daily movement, household structure, and schooling choices. It offers planners another way to think about keeping children learning during a pandemic.
plos-pone-0007321:
Olga Renner, Simone Harsch, Elke Schaeffeler, and colleagues studied a bile acid transporter gene and gallstones in 2009. Gallstone disease, or cholelithiasis, has many causes. Several mechanisms of stone formation had been proposed, including reduced activity of a transporter that reclaims bile acids in the ileum.

That transporter is made by the gene SLC10A2. Earlier work found lower expression of the gene in gallstone carriers. The authors test a variant of SLC10A2 as a risk factor. Their PLOS ONE finding links inherited transporter differences to gallstone formation in patients studied.
openalex-w1867913521: Breast cancer isn't just human — dogs get mammary tumors too. Salas and colleagues' 2015 PLoS ONE study mapped the epidemiology of mammary tumors in female dogs diagnosed from 2002 to 2012. The study defined risk factors for a growing animal health problem.
openalex-w2019595721: A five-quark particle — long predicted, never seen. The LHCb team's 2015 paper reported J/ψp bumps consistent with pentaquark states in Λb0 → J/ψ K− p decays. The exotic signals rewrote the quark-model rulebook at last.
openalex-w2032080021: Chagas drugs disappoint — combos may do better. A 2013 study tested benznidazole and posaconazole together and in sequence against experimental Chagas disease in mice. The paired approach beat either drug alone, with fewer dropouts.
openalex-w2057889321: Hydrogen sulfide is a poison — and a messenger. A 2012 study measured how the gas enters lipid membranes. The work showed how cell walls shape the gas's biological role in tissues.

openalex-w2089584121: Crowds are mostly friends walking together. Moussaïd and colleagues' 2010 study found up to 70% of people in crowds move in social groups — and measured how group walking shapes crowd dynamics. The work rewrote crowd models around friendship.

openalex-w2108565421: Belly infections kill worldwide — CIAOW counted them. A 2014 study gathered data on complicated belly infections worldwide. The 68-site, six-month study mapped the infections' toll and treatments from October 2012 to March 2013 — the definitive picture.
plos-pone-0006321:
A yeast that causes meningitis in vulnerable patients coats its proteins with sugars as a first decorating step. plos-pone-0009721:
Trypanosoma cruzi is the parasite that causes Chagas disease in the Americas. Igor Cestari and Marcel Ramirez studied how some strains slip into host cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The parasite spreads to people mainly through biting insects.

The immune system's complement arm should clear the parasite's infective forms from the blood. For resistant strains, that clearance worked poorly, letting the parasites reach cells and invade them. Weak clearance thus helps explain why some strains infect so well. The finding points to an early battle the immune system often loses.
openalex-w2440323021: Taro feeds millions across the tropics, yet where it came from and how it spread remain murky. The genetic map clarifies taro's origins and the ancient human migrations that carried this staple around the world.
openalex-w2627092521: Everyone sells 'prebiotics,' but what does the word actually mean? openalex-w2788689621: Climate science runs on radiation measurements — and the Baseline Surface Radiation Network has collected them since 1992. openalex-w4401815221: Semaglutide cuts cardiovascular events in obesity — but heart failure patients were an open question. europmc-pmc3143121: Cell power plants got a microplate test. This 2011 paper measures mitochondrial respiration in microplates with tiny samples. The authors' method cut sample needs. Their work powered the Seahorse era. Old methods needed far more tissue. Drug screens now run hundreds of wells.

22149-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Carter G. Woodson founded The Journal of Negro History in 1916 to give Black history scholarly standing. Volume 6, for 1921, gathers a year's articles, reviews, and documents. One essay opens bluntly: the citizenship of the Negro in America is a fiction. The Constitution promises him every right, the writer argues, while the federal government evades its duty to guard those rights.

Other pieces study slavery, Reconstruction, Black soldiers, and African backgrounds. Woodson's journal printed the evidence on which later history would build. In 1921 almost no white university would touch these subjects. The volume shows Woodson's enterprise at work: exact, angry, and determined to make a record.
arxiv-2601-07421:
Nat Sothanaphan and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with resolution of erdős problem #728. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We provide a writeup of a resolution of Erdős Problem #728. This is the first Erdős problem (a problem proposed by Paul Erdős which has been collected in.

The Erdős Problems website [ 3 ] ) regarded as fully resolved autonomously by an AI system. The system in question is a combination of GPT-5. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-08121: Mykola Pinchuk asks whether a popular XGBoost setting hides ratio-based patterns from the model. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that many real signals appear only after raw measures are combined. Ratios and rates are common cases of such combined signal. A boosted tree cannot form a ratio directly, so it must mimic one through coordinated splits. Pinchuk studies whether sampling columns inside each tree makes that coordination harder to learn. The question matters for practitioners who rely on default subsampling settings in applied prediction tasks.
arxiv-2601-08321:
Lichen Ma and co-authors present UM-Text, a unified model for image understanding and visual text editing. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses editing text inside images through natural language instructions. The task has drawn growing attention as image generation has advanced fast.

The central challenge is to grasp both the instruction and the reference image fully. The edited text must then match the image in style, or the result looks pasted on. A single model that both understands images and edits their text could simplify design tools. Posters, signs, and product shots all carry text that users often need to change without reshooting.
arxiv-2601-07521:
Stefano Biagi and colleagues study a critical equation that mixes two kinds of diffusion. Their 2026 preprint combines a standard Laplacian with a fractional Laplacian in one operator. The twist is the sign: the fractional part carries the so-called wrong sign. That makes it a nonlocal disturbance of the purely local case. Superposition operators of this kind arise in modern analysis.

Critical problems sit at the edge where standard methods for existence of solutions can fail. Adding a wrong-sign nonlocal term changes the balance further. The authors work out what this mixed operator does in that critical setting. The paper is aimed at specialists in partial differential equations. It clarifies how local and nonlocal effects interact when neither behaves as usual.
arxiv-2601-07621:
E. Bednarczuk and colleagues study how to match patterns hidden in three-dimensional point clouds. Their 2026 preprint addresses comparing and aligning spatial point configurations that describe local topography. Each pattern is split into arms. Along each arm, the authors define a normalized finite-difference operator. That operator measures local changes in height relative to the flat layout of the pattern.

Point pattern search matters when the same shape must be found across large terrain data. Height changes along arms give a signature that survives some noise and shift. The team's construction turns a geometric matching problem into comparable measurements. Readers in geomatics and pattern recognition get a method shaped for structured patterns in real landscapes. The work comes from Polish research institutes.
arxiv-2601-07921:
Simone Biondini and colleagues map which flavor patterns of dark matter survive current data. Their question is direct: what flavor structure of t-channel thermal dark matter fits flavour physics and direct detection bounds? They chart the space of hypotheses using flavour symmetries and their breaking patterns. The focus then narrows to scenarios where the dark matter fermion and its scalar mediator are flavour singlets. Those fall into rank-one flavour violation. Their 2026 preprint draws the map.

Flavor structure decides how dark matter couples to the generations of quarks and leptons. Different patterns leave different fingerprints in rare decays and underground detectors. Charting the whole space shows where future experiments should look. Singlet scenarios are attractive for their simplicity and testability. The paper serves particle theorists and experimentalists planning searches. It turns a broad model space into a set of concrete surviving options.
arxiv-2601-07221: Jongwon Ryu and six co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on changing a photo by words. A user types a phrase that names what should change. The tool must make that change and no more. Parts the words do not touch must stay as they were. Past tools can warp the scene as they work. The team guides the change by the gap in sense between the source photo and the words. The aim is tight control of each trait that shifts.
arxiv-2601-08421: Juno Kim, Jihun Yun, Jason Lee, and Kwang-Sung Jun wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how language models learn from likes and dislikes. In on-policy learning, the model trains on text it made itself, as it goes. Such methods, like online direct policy optimization, can beat offline ones by a wide gap. The authors track how the coverage of the sampling policy shifts in training. Coverage means how much of its own output range the model gets to learn from as it trains.
arxiv-2601-08721:
Roberto Garrone writes about how small funds add theme based parts to a main core fund. Most teams judge such parts by past gains or by how easy they are to trade. Garrone says that path fits big funds, not small ones. For a small fund, the real limits are fixed costs and hard to undo choices.

He puts ease of use first, before any hope of high gains. A part should be added only if the fund can hold it, check it, and leave it with low cost and low fuss. The goal is a fund that stays sound over time. A reader gets a clear rule for when to say no to a new theme part.
arxiv-2601-09621:
Sidan A and Tom Banks revisit how spacetime regions map to quantum subsystems in holographic theories. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns causal diamonds and large-N scaling in AdS/CFT. Quantum field theory taught that a causal diamond, a region bounded by light travel, matches a subsystem of the global theory.

Work by Jacobson, Fischler, Susskind, and Bousso suggested the subsystem carries a density matrix of finite entropy. That hint came from black hole physics. The authors examine how the picture scales as N grows large. The stakes are the rules by which gravity emerges from a boundary theory.
arxiv-2601-09821:
Gloria Henríquez and five co-authors forecast winter surges of sick children in Santiago, Chile. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds an alert-based model for peaks of acute respiratory infections. These infections are a major cause of child hospitalization in Chile, with sharp winter rises.

The model joins SIR epidemic dynamics with historical trends. It aims to predict both the timing and the size of hospitalization peaks. Advance warning lets hospitals staff their wards and stock needed supplies before the winter rush. Alert thresholds turn the forecast into decisions managers can act on.
arxiv-2601-09921:
Kai Zhang and a large team of co authors work on quantum error checks. A quantum machine makes errors as it runs. A decoder must check the error signs fast and fix them in time. Neural nets can beat older hand made rules at this task.

The snag is speed. Past neural decoders do not work in parallel well. They can fall behind the stream of error signs from a real chip. The team built a net that learns to split the work and run in parallel. It aims to keep up in real time. That step is key for a quantum machine that can run long tasks.
arxiv-2601-10021:
Eckhard Meinrenken gives a first guide to weights along a sub shape. In this field, a weight grades how fast a thing grows near a part of a space. The idea came from work by Melrose. He used a name that tied it to near even growth.

Meinrenken and Loizides later gave the idea its present name. The guide pulls in work by many hands since then. It sets out the base terms and the main facts. Such a guide helps new readers enter a field that grew in parts. It also shows where the main open paths lie.
arxiv-2601-10221:
Byung Gyu Chae builds one field theory for three acts: learn, infer, and emerge. These acts are oft split across fields. Brain work, stats, and nets each use their own frame. Chae seeks one frame that holds all three.

He starts from a spare random flow rule. From it, he builds a field form of the MSRJD type. That form is a known tool for random flows. In his frame, learn and infer come from the same rule. Emergence then shows how large acts grow from small ones. The work is a bid for one tongue for these acts.
arxiv-2601-10321:
Warren Jouanneau, Emma Jouffroy, and Marc Palyart match people to jobs in real time. A CV can be long and rich in form. It may also be in one of many tongues. A brief for a job has the same traits. A match tool must scan both fast and well.

The team built a re rank model on a new cross attention form. Late cross attention reads the pair near the end of the net. It splits both texts into parts to hold long inputs. Cost stays low. The model is tuned with grades from a large model, set to a firm scale.
arxiv-2601-10621:
H. Liu, O. Stein, A. Vaxman, M. Ben-Chen, and M. Kazhdan present a new way to handle vector fields on triangle meshes. Vector fields on a surface matter for tasks like texture flow, simulation, and shape design. Their method is extrinsic, meaning it uses the way the mesh sits in space. It starts from a Phong map that assigns smooth normals at every point.

Using the Rodrigues rotation formula, they carry vectors from mesh corners into the inside of each triangle. That builds smooth bases for fields that vary across the surface. The scheme aims to be both simple and robust for geometry software. It gives graphics and simulation tools a fresh base for field-based effects.
arxiv-2601-10721:
Xinyu Li and co-authors survey collaborative continuum robots. A continuum robot bends along its whole length, like an elephant trunk, instead of at stiff joints. Its compact build, softness, and flex make it fit for tight and delicate spaces. Teaming several of them up forms a collaborative system.

Working together, the robots gain reach, load capacity, and stability beyond what one can do. They also adapt to more kinds of tasks. The survey gathers what is known about these teams and where they fall short. It serves engineers who design soft robots for medicine, inspection, and other jobs where rigid arms cannot go.
arxiv-2601-10821:
Nikita Lvov proves a universality result for random matrices over finite local rings. Random matrix theory studies the traits of matrices filled by chance. Universality says some traits stay the same across many random choices. Lvov looks at the cokernel of a random matrix, an algebraic shadow of the matrix that records its divisibility structure.

Rather than the moment method, he uses the Lindeberg replacement technique, swapping entries one at a time. The statement he proves is quantitative, with explicit rates. Finite local rings sit behind coding theory and number theory. Universality there tells us that random constructions behave alike, a fact builders of codes and ciphers can lean on.
arxiv-2601-11021:
Kecheng Cai and co-authors fight spurious correlations in graph interpretability. Interpretable graph learning seeks the nodes and edges that drive a model's call on a graph task. Many methods exist, and benchmark datasets have been proposed to judge them. The risk is that an explanation latches onto patterns that merely ride along with the true cause.

The authors use self-reflection to combat such false leads. A method that checks its own explanation can drop edges that do not hold up. Trustworthy explanations matter wherever graph models screen molecules, fraud, or disease. The work helps keep interpretability honest in a field where a pretty explanation can be a wrong one.
arxiv-2601-11321:
Varun Venkatesh, Farzan Vafa, Martin Pedersen, and Amin Doostmohammadi study spiral waves. Their 2026 preprint puts such waves on folded surfaces. Spiral waves mark systems that sit far from equilibrium. They show up in chemistry, biology, and active matter alike.

In living systems, waves often run on curved or folded sheets. The shape of the sheet is rarely treated as a live factor. The team treats shape as part of the dynamics itself. Forces that arise far from equilibrium can steer the spirals. Those forces link the wave's path to the folds below. The work hints that tissue shape may guide real waves. That idea could matter for hearts, brains, and growing embryos.
arxiv-2601-11421:
Ziyu Wang and eight coauthors set 100 fine tasks for embodied AI agents. Their 2026 preprint names the set The Great March 100. Robot learning has grown fast, with many datasets and methods. Task design in those datasets often lacks a shared logic.

Loose task design raises a fair doubt for the field. Do current tasks truly push agent skills to grow? The team's 100 tasks are detail-oriented by design. Each task tests fine control and care in the real world. A shared, principled set lets labs compare agents fairly. It also shows which skills still lag in robots. The bench aims to steer robot learning toward real competence.
arxiv-2601-11521:
Andrew Sullivan, Jack Dinsmore, and Roger Romani measure X-ray polarization from a pulsar shock. Their 2026 preprint studies redback pulsar J1723-2837. Spider pulsars host shocks inside the binary system itself. The pulsar wind slams into matter from its companion star.

The shock emits non-thermal synchrotron X-rays in response. Fast electrons and positrons in the shock produce that glow. Magnetic reconnection likely energizes those particles in the shock. Light curves from such shocks show a double-peaked form. That form is well characterized in several spider systems. Polarization adds a new probe of the shock's field. It can test how reconnection orders the magnetic field there.
arxiv-2601-11621:
Mahesh Ramani computes one Catalan number at an unprecedented scale. The 2026 preprint gives a two-phase algorithm for exact values. Catalan numbers count many classic combinatorial structures. Their exact values grow to huge sizes very fast.

The target index is n equal to 2,050,572,903 here. The result aims at 1,234,567,890 decimal digits in length. No prior computation reached Catalan numbers at this scale. A two-phase method makes the giant arithmetic tractable. Exact digits at this size test both math and machines. Such feats check big-integer libraries against known truth. They also set records for exact combinatorics computing.
arxiv-2601-13321:
Claudio Agostini, Fernando Barrera, and Vincenzo Dimonte prove a no go result on broad forms of measure. Measure theory gives size to sets. A long ask was if it can be stretched to non separable spaces in a full way. Parts, such as the ideal of null sets, have been stretched in past work.

The open part was a sound notion of measure at a scale past a given cardinal, in the broad set theory frame. The team shows that aim fails in the wide class they treat, past the old frame. A clean no go can save years of hunt. It tells maths staff where to stop and which weaker aims may still live.
arxiv-2601-13421:
Alexander Barzykin models how foreign exchange dealers set prices while their hedges move the market. A dealer quotes a buy and a sell price to each client. To hold risk in check, a dealer can skew quotes to draw flow one way. A dealer can also hedge in the interbank market.

A hedge gives a firm out come but costs fees and shifts the price as it trades, a transient impact that fades. Barzykin weighs quote skew next to hedge in one model. The model shows how a dealer should split the two as flow and risk shift. For trade desks, that split is a day to day call with real cost.
arxiv-2601-12821:
Yan Jiang, Hongyu Liu, Fanbo Sun, and Yajuan Wang study sub wavelength resonances in layered elastic media. Their setting is two dimensional, with multiple layers of material. The media have high contrasts in both Lame parameters and density. High contrast can trap waves at scales far below their wavelength.

Sub wavelength resonances matter for sensing, imaging, and energy devices. The team state fourfold contributions to the theory of these resonances. Layered elastic systems model real composites and geological strata. Knowing where resonances sit helps design materials that steer elastic waves. It also helps read signals that pass through such media. The work sits in applied mathematics and wave physics.
arxiv-2601-12921:
Adimulya Kartiyasa, Bao Gia Cao, and Boyang Li improve how language models understand Indonesian cultures. Efforts to teach models Indonesian cultural knowledge have intensified of late. One attractive source has been largely overlooked: local social science journals. Such journals likely contain substantial cultural studies written from a native perspective.

The team inject knowledge from those journals into language models. Native scholarship can correct the outsider framing that web data often carries. Better cultural understanding should make models safer and more useful for Indonesian users. The approach may generalize to other cultures with strong local journals. It treats regional academia as a first class data source.
arxiv-2601-13621:
Siyuan Chen, Karan Jani, and Thomas Kephart take stock of entropy tied to black holes in 2026. Black holes hold more entropy, a measure of hidden states, than all else in the seen universe. Waves from merging black holes, caught by LIGO and Virgo, have shown a mass range not known before. That new range changes the count of what black holes hold.

The team updates the cosmic entropy budget with this new mass data. A sound budget helps test ideas on how the universe grows and cools. It also sharpens the puzzle of why entropy sits so heavily in black holes. Their tally gives later work a fresh base.
arxiv-2601-14021:
Omer Abdelmajeed Idris Mohammed builds access control that watches how code was launched, not just by whom in 2026. Modern operating systems offer strong mandatory access control tools. They largely reason about who executes code, not how execution originates. A process run remotely, locally, or by a background service is often treated the same once privileges are gained.

That sameness complicates security reasoning after a compromise. Attackers can abuse sensitive system interfaces from odd origins. OAMAC is origin-aware mandatory access control. It aims at practical post-compromise attack surface reduction for real systems. The aim is to block abuse at the door it came in, not just by the name on the key. That shift in view may shape how new systems check trust.
arxiv-2601-14121:
Jonathan Tonglet and co-authors help journalists pin down where and when a news photo was taken in 2026. Identifying a news image's context is crucial for credible stories. It also helps debunk misinformation that recycles old photos. Many existing methods rely on reverse image search engines.

These tools often fail to return results, limiting practical use. The team addresses the hard scenario where reverse search evidence is unavailable. Their NewsRECON retrieves news articles to contextualize an image instead. Article matches can date and place a photo when search engines cannot.
arxiv-2601-14221:
Mohak Goyal and co-authors argue deliberation research misses a key dimension of opinion change in 2026. Deliberative processes are often judged by polarization alone. Polarization can rise or fall as people talk. That lens misses whether deliberation reshuffles who agrees with whom.

Opinion mixing is their name for that reshuffling dimension. A process might move everyone in parallel, preserving the pre-deliberation rank ordering. Or it might scramble alliances while averages stay put. The team calls mixing a more diagnostic measure of social influence in deliberation. Rank shifts tell a tale that mean views hide. Two talks can end with the same mean but a quite distinct map of who stands with whom.
arxiv-2601-14421:
Jay Armas and Akash Jain study spin fluids in this 2026 paper. Relativistic spin fluids carry conserved currents that come from microscopic models. Those currents are known to violate local thermodynamic relations, the basic rules that tie heat, pressure, and flow. That clash signals a flaw in how the fluid theory is framed.

The authors give a systematic analysis of pseudo-gauge improvements in ideal spin hydrodynamics. A pseudo-gauge is a choice in how spin and energy currents are split. They identify a family of pseudo-gauges where standard thermodynamic relations hold. Readers get a cleaner base for modeling spinning matter, such as the plasma made in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2601-15621:
The Qwen Team presents a family of text-to-speech models in a 2026 arXiv technical report. The series is called Qwen3-TTS. The models are described as multilingual, controllable, robust, and built for streaming. Streaming means speech starts before the full text is processed. That suits live assistants and interactive tools. Two control features headline the report.

First comes voice cloning from a three-second sample. A short clip can define a new voice. Second comes description-based control. A user can describe the voice they want in words. Together these allow both brand-new voices and fine tweaks to output speech. Technical reports like this serve builders who may adopt the models. They also stake the team's claims in a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2601-15721:
Xinda Chen and a large team study the neglected half of recommendation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Knowing what users like is fairly straightforward. Knowing what they dislike is harder, and far less studied. Platforms increasingly add explicit negative feedback tools. Those signals can refine recommendation models. Their system is called CoNRec, short for context-discerning negative recommendation.

Large language models drive the approach, per the title. Context matters because a dislike can be narrow. A user may reject one item yet love its neighbors. Reading dislike with context avoids over-blocking. For platforms, better use of negative signals means fewer annoying suggestions. For users, it means the not-interested button finally teaches the system something real.
arxiv-2601-15921:
Shao-Ping Li and Apostolos Pilaftsis highlight a new channel for making the cosmic matter excess in a 2026 arXiv paper. Leptogenesis explains why matter beat antimatter in the early universe. Low-scale versions work near energies we can reach. The known channels use mixing and oscillation of massive singlet neutrinos. The authors show a thermal resonant channel beyond those. They show it is always present in a common setting.

The setting is the heat-driven decay of the Higgs to leptons and relativistic sterile neutrinos. Flavor oscillations in the lepton doublet are made by heat there. Those oscillations can make the new channel dominant. A dominant new channel changes what tests should see. Low-scale leptogenesis can be tested, so sharper theory helps aim those tests.
arxiv-2601-14921:
Sarat Ahmad, Maryam Hafeez, and Syed Ali Raza Zaidi ask how robots can use vision-language models without the cloud. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at models that read both images and words. Such models help robots perceive a scene and act on spoken or written cues.

On a real robot, these models run into hard limits. They are slow, the onboard hardware is weak, and cloud use brings privacy risks. The authors point to edge computing within 6G networks as a way out. Open RAN and edge servers bring the compute close to the robot.
arxiv-2601-15221:
Hanlei Guo, Jiahao Shao, and co-authors generate city scenes by way of flat images. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with 3D urban scene generation with diffusion models. Making a whole city block that looks real is much harder than making one object.

Pure 3D diffusion tends to lose fine surface detail. Pure 2D diffusion keeps the detail but gives up camera control. The authors present ScenDi, a cascade that goes from 3D to 2D in stages. The design aims to keep both the fine detail and the control over camera viewpoints.
arxiv-2601-16321:
Sima Amirkhani and coauthors study love scams that target young teens in Iran. Their 2026 preprint deals with online date scams as a harm to youth. Past work in the West finds most prey are of mid age. It is not known if teens face the same risk in lands with teen wed norms. Parental hopes add push that the title quote makes plain.

The team asks how scams use those hopes to trap teens. Trap paths may turn on wed hopes held by kin. Clear paths would guide guards for teens in such lands. The work is the first close look at this risk there. It serves teams who guard youth online.
arxiv-2601-16421:
Gautham Reddy and coauthors map radio reach for drones with a coder tool. Their 2026 preprint, named TransfoREM, deals with cell reach for craft in flight. Ground cell nets aim their reach at ground users first. Craft in the air get reach from weak side lobes of those poles. Weak reach leaves gaps and drops in flight paths.

Maps of reach in 3D tell where craft can stay linked. The team builds those maps with a coder led tool. It learns from past reach data in real nets. Good maps let teams plan safe drone routes in town air. They also show where new poles would help most.
arxiv-2601-16821:
Harrison Katz models shares that must sum to a whole over time. Such share sets track things like budgets or diets by part. Big shocks can break the trend of those shares. Wars, laws, or market crashes cause such breaks. Old tools mark breaks with blunt flags that can't look ahead. His 2026 preprint builds a model that bends with breaks.

His model shifts the share path in a set aim. It can project shares past the break point. Past tools could not do that with their flags. Sound share paths aid plans in health, trade, and food work. The model gives those plans a firmer base.
arxiv-2601-17021:
Muhammad Aarash and Hassan Jaleel build fund picks that learn from past misses. Fund work must trade risk gainst gain in each pick. Long holds make that trade more hard. Their 2026 preprint pairs chatbots with a no-regret learn rule. Mood signs from markets join the mix as well. Smart clusters group stocks for the pick step.

The frame aims at high Sharpe marks for calm funds. Sharpe marks weigh gain by the risk took. Chatbot hedge calls add a shield in bad weeks. Such frames may aid funds that serve risk-shy savers. They blend AI sense with strict learn rules.
arxiv-2601-17221:
Dominik Winecki and Arnab Nandi built a system called Vidformer for work with video data. In video-native querying, users do not just get tables back. They get video back, with clips joined and data laid over frames. That last step, rendering, is the slow part. It is slower than the query work itself, and today it runs through slow scripts.

Vidformer adds fast, drop-in rendering to that flow. Users state what they want in a plain, declarative way. The system then speeds up how result videos are made. For teams that search large video sets, this cuts wait time. It makes hands-on video search feel quick and direct.
arxiv-2601-17521:
Dean Kraizberg studies two-player games on infinite trees and their link to prefix codes. Players move in turns along the tree's branches. The trees here are full and regular. The winning set is open in the product topology. Open games have known ties to code design. Prefix codes are codes where no codeword starts another. They run all data compression.

Kraizberg seeks sharp winning criteria for such games. Clear criteria tell who wins from a given start. They also expose how game shape mirrors code shape. That mirror can move results between fields. Game theory and information theory both gain. The work is pure, but its roots touch daily tech.
arxiv-2601-17621:
Tim Ritmeester proposes a new kind of statistical interval. It sits between Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist ones. A standard credible interval claims a set level of belief from full data. Ritmeester weakens that claim in a set way. Having seen only the interval, not the full data, we should still hold at least the stated belief in it.

The design uses one-dimensional priors. It aims for finite-sample claims that stay honest. A middle ground could serve fields split by the old debate. Health and policy work need intervals users can trust. Finite-sample care matters most when data is scarce. The proposal gives statisticians a fresh option to test.
arxiv-2601-17721:
Huy Trinh, Elliot Creager, and George Shaker detect quiet human presence with radar. Radar sensing guards privacy better than cameras or wearables. Long-term care is a prime use case. The hard case is semi-static presence. A person lying, sitting, or standing still gives only subtle micro-motions. Low-resolution SIMO FMCW radar buries near-zero Doppler energy under static clutter.

Their method amplifies respiration in the Doppler domain. Breathing is a steady sign of life even at rest. Lifting that signal above clutter makes presence reads reliable. Care staff gain a quiet monitor that respects dignity. The work pairs signal craft with a real care need.
arxiv-2601-17821:
Jose Segovia-Martin studies how cooperation can get stuck in games played on a grid. His 2026 preprint returns to a classic setup, the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma of Nowak and May. In that setup, players copy the best neighbor they see. Past runs show cooperation falling off a cliff near a key temptation value. The author looks at the shapes that form on the lattice at that point.

Those shapes act as traps set by the layout of the game. Once play falls into a trap, cooperation has a hard time coming back. Naming the trap helps explain why a smooth change in payoffs can cause a sudden drop. The work speaks to the wider study of how norms hold or break.
arxiv-2601-17921:
Yi Zhao, Qinghua Yao, Xinyuan Song, and Wei Zhu refine a cheap way to tune large language models. Their 2026 preprint is about LoRA, which adapts a model by adding small low-rank parts. The standard form gives each part the same rank. Later work showed that picking ranks with care boosts scores. The question is how to split a fixed rank budget across the model.

The team's method, ShapLoRA, borrows the Shapley value from game theory. That value scores how much each part adds to the whole. Ranks then flow to the parts that earn them. Smarter ranks mean better tuning for the same cost. The idea helps groups that cannot afford full fine-tuning.
arxiv-2601-19121:
Guilin Zhang and three co-authors put language models in charge of a team of recommendation agents. A recommender must serve many goals at once while obeying hard business rules. A shop, for instance, may demand that each list span several sellers and meet fairness and coverage floors.

The models act as orchestrators, steering sub agents while keeping every rule in force. Letting a model juggle goals is easy; keeping it inside hard limits is the hard part. Systems that do both could tune feeds in real time without breaking the rules firms must keep.
arxiv-2601-19221:
Liu Xiao rethinks the inner state of recurrent language models as something that can be edited. Modern recurrent nets like RWKV model nearby text well and keep a fixed size state, a core edge over transformers. Yet few studies treat that state as a store of knowledge that can be read or changed.

The work, DREAMSTATE, diffuses both states and parameters, borrowing the gradual noise and cleanup of image diffusion. If a recurrent model's state can be edited like a file, builders gain a new lever for fixing facts and behavior. The study opens that lever to its first close look.
arxiv-2601-19421:
Josh Susak, Yifu Liu, Pascal Jansen, and Mark Colley design car assistants that speak first, at the right moments. In-vehicle conversational assistants mostly wait for the driver to ask. The next step is proactive help: the car offers or starts an action before being asked, without nagging or distracting.

The team tunes that proactive behavior with multi objective Bayesian optimization, balancing gains in driver experience against costs. A car that speaks up must earn each interruption. Their method seeks settings where the help lands as timely rather than pushy, a design question every smart car will face.
arxiv-2601-19621:
Nagula Venkata Anirudh, Sachidananda Behera, and Kirti Chandra Sahu simulate what happens when a drop hits a liquid surface. Real drops are rarely perfect spheres. Their shape as they fall changes how they splash. The team runs three-dimensional computer simulations of non-spherical drops striking a still liquid film.

They vary the drop's shape and its impact speed across a wide range. The simulations reveal several distinct behaviours, from smooth spreading to two kinds of splashing. In some cases the drop throws up a canopy, and finger-like jets at the crown can turn unstable. The authors map which behaviour occurs for each mix of shape and speed. Such maps help engineers predict splashes in printing, spraying, and fuel systems.
arxiv-2601-19821:
Kun Li, Michael Ying Yang, and Sami Sebastian Brandt build systems that answer questions about music videos. Audio-visual question answering demands joint reasoning over sound, image, and text. For music, the audio track is not background; it carries the melody, rhythm, and instruments the question may target. Many existing systems lean heavily on the visual stream and underuse the sound.

Their method is guided by the query itself. It models interactions across space, time, and frequency in the audio-visual features. Frequency matters for music in a way it does not for speech scenes. Letting the question steer the fusion should focus the model on the right moments. The work pushes multimodal systems to treat music as a first-class signal.
arxiv-2601-19921:
Xiaochen Zhu and five colleagues dissect multi-agent debate, a popular trick for improving language model answers. Several model instances argue, then settle on an answer. The method costs more compute than a simple majority vote. Recent work shows plain debate often underperforms that cheaper baseline.

The authors ask what role confidence and diversity play in the outcome. Under uniform agents with uniform belief updates, debate preserves expected correctness, so it cannot reliably help. Variety among agents and well-used confidence signals are the candidate fixes. The analysis explains many disappointing results in the literature. It also tells builders when debate is worth its price and when voting suffices.
arxiv-2601-20121:
Jiaming Wang and five colleagues study a long-noted pattern in the solar wind, the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. The magnetic field carried by the wind shows a one-over-f pattern of power across low frequencies. That band runs from near the period of the Sun's spin down to much shorter times.

The authors compare synthetic data with real solar wind records to test ideas about how the pattern arises. Their focus is on superposition, the adding of many signals into one. Knowing the source of this pattern helps physicists read spacecraft data and model the space weather that reaches Earth.
arxiv-2601-20321:
A team from Beihang University, ShanghaiTech University, and partner institutes studies how to give robot vision-language-action models a sense of touch. These models are strong generalists for manipulation, but they rely almost wholly on vision. Contact-rich tasks need precise force control and physical reasoning that sight alone cannot supply.

The authors align tactile and force signals with the model's vision and language inputs. Their aim is force-aware manipulation, where the robot adjusts its grip and pressure as contact changes. Robots that can feel what they hold would be safer around fragile objects and people.
arxiv-2601-20521:
Jose Antonio Moreno and seven colleagues measure the superconducting density of states in nitridized aluminum thin films. Nitride-based superconductors often outperform the bare metal in devices, such as sensors for cosmic radiation. Niobium and titanium nitrides have already improved devices for quantum technology.

The authors turn to aluminum treated with nitrogen and probe how its states are distributed in energy. That distribution governs how the film behaves in circuits and detectors. Aluminum is the workhorse of superconducting quantum devices, so a nitride route to better films could raise the quality of qubits and sensors alike.
arxiv-2601-20621:
Agnieszka Bodzenta, Tomasz Pełka, and Dario Weißmann study the saturation of algebraic surfaces. The saturation of a surface is its maximal open embedding whose complement has dimension zero, so only isolated points are added. For schemes, the notion was introduced by Bodzenta with A. Bondal.

They showed that a surface's saturation can be recovered from the category of reflexive sheaves on it. That is a striking bridge: a geometric completion read off from a category of sheaves. The present work develops this theory of saturation for algebraic surfaces. That is a strong claim, and the proof is the heart of the work. It gives the field a new way to build a whole from a part.
arxiv-2601-18621:
Fernando Belchior and Roberto Maluf study when two maths forms of the same field world are in truth the same. The world at hand is a pared-down form of light and field maths that keeps just one line of space. On top of it sits a cross term that joins two kinds of field. One form of the world has strict rules for what counts as the same state. The next form drops those rules.

The pair show the two forms match when no fields are at play. They prove the match in two ways: by a straight check of how each form moves, and by a master form that holds both. Such proofs of match let staff pick the form that is less hard to use. They also guard against the same world being counted twice as two finds.
arxiv-2601-21621:
Matéo Mahaut and Marco Baroni ask whether vision models not only end at similar inner representations but also get there the same way. A growing body of work says bigger models converge to shared, almost universal representations. That holds despite different training goals, data, and input types.

The authors study the intermediate steps that lead to those shared endpoints. Do models pass through the same stages, or only meet at the finish? The answer bears on whether there is one natural way to process images. It also affects how safely parts can be swapped between models.
arxiv-2601-22321:
Dominic Payne and a large team track bends in the solar wind near a key border called the Alfvén surface. Inside that border, the Sun's field rules the flow; outside, the flow breaks free. Their 2026 preprint studies sharp magnetic bends, known as switchbacks, on both sides.

They sort the bends by a shared angle measure. A thin shift layer near the border seems to steer how the bends grow and change. That clue helps explain where switchbacks are born. It also guides reads of data from probes that dive near the Sun.
arxiv-2601-22421:
AlexKen Lee and Keyun Wu ask if supersymmetry could leave a hum in the background of gravitational waves. That background hum may have been born in the reheating era, just after the cosmos' first burst of growth. Their 2026 preprint builds a sample contact point for the idea.

The contact links one inflaton field to the D-term parts of a pair of chiral superfields. From it they work out how strong the hum might be. Future detectors could then look for that shape. A match would be a rare clue to physics past the standard model.
arxiv-2601-21921:
Zhouyou Gu and co-authors plan the backbone of future satellite internet. Laser links between low Earth orbit satellites can carry huge capacity, but managing them is hard. Terminals are few, they must aim mechanically, and the network's shape changes rapidly as satellites move.

The team studies the joint problem of establishing connections and routing traffic in real time across mega-constellations. Their 2026 preprint uses duality-guided graph learning, letting optimization theory steer a learning system. Good joint decisions mean fewer dropped links and better use of scarce laser terminals. As constellations grow to thousands of satellites, planning methods that keep up in real time become a condition for the whole service to work.
arxiv-2601-22021:
Yu Chen, Genjiu Xu, Sinan Feng, and Chaoqian Wang model what happens after a disaster, when resources are scarce and infrastructure is paralyzed. Recovery depends on coordination between shelters that hold supplies and the victims who need them. The two groups influence each other as aid moves and needs change.

The authors build a two-layer network model of that feedback. One layer represents shelters, the other victims, and cooperative behavior evolves on the coupled network as resources are redistributed. Their 2026 preprint studies how cooperation emerges or collapses under different conditions. Insights like these could help planners design aid systems that encourage trust and sharing when both are hardest to sustain.
arxiv-2601-20821:
Katherine Paulson, Taylor Okonek, and Jon Wakefield build a better way to estimate how many young children die. Their 2026 paper presents a survival framework for child mortality rates. Child mortality is a key sign of population health. Yet many countries lack strong vital registration to measure it well. Rates must then be pieced together from surveys and other partial sources.

Large efforts already model these rates. The United Nations group for child mortality estimation and the Global Burden of Disease study both do so. The authors' framework uses multiple data types at once. It targets the standard summaries: neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality. Better estimates guide health spending where records are thin. The work helps ensure that scarce data still yields rates that leaders can trust.
arxiv-2601-20921:
Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarioglu propose a new index tool for data stored in DNA. Their 2026 paper adds a stochastic primitive for molecular archives. Random access is a central bottleneck in DNA-based data storage. Current systems fetch records by PCR or other multi-step lab work. Those steps do not support fast, parallel, content-based queries. The authors aim to close that gap.

They introduce the Holographic Bloom Filter, or HBF. It encodes key-pointer links as a single high-dimensional vector. A query can probe that vector at once, with no lab work per lookup. The design promises database-like search over DNA stores. The paper lays out the primitive and its promise. It sketches a future where DNA stores answer questions at electronic speed.
arxiv-2512-01321:
Juan Hernandez and co-authors test a learning method when many agents act at once. The method, called Never Give Up, rewards an agent for finding new states. It mixes that drive with scores from the task. That mix helps when rewards are rare.

The team moved the method from one agent to many agents. They tried it in a tag game from the PettingZoo set. In that game, agents chase and flee in a small world. Early tests show how the drive to explore holds up when peers learn too. The work is a first step, not a final word.
arxiv-2512-01421:
Valentin Duruisseaux, Jean Kossaifi, and Anima Anandkumar explain Fourier neural operators in plain terms. Equations for fluids, heat, and stress govern much of science. Solving them needs fine grids and many repeats. That makes each solve slow and costly.

Neural operators learn the solve step itself. Fourier types do that work in the frequency domain for speed. The guide lays out how they work with real cases. It shows when they shine and when they fail. A clear guide helps engineers pick the right tool for fast physics forecasts. Worked cases span fluids and waves, so a reader can see the same operator idea pay off across more than one physics field.
arxiv-2512-00721:
Hiroko Okada, Wako Aoki, Nozomu Tominaga, and Satoshi Honda report on a very old, metal-poor star in a 2025 astronomy paper. The star, known by its survey name SMSS 0224-5737, holds very little of the heavy elements later stars carry. Such stars preserve clues about the first stars and how elements formed.

The team measured abundances for many chemical elements in the star's light. Several elements, including nitrogen, oxygen, vanadium, zinc, and barium, are reported with fresh values. Others get upper limits rather than firm values. The pattern points to a weak form of the rapid process that builds heavy elements in extreme events.
arxiv-2512-00821:
Michael Kerber and Elena Xinyi Wang wrote a 2025 paper on measuring shape differences. The Persistent Homology Transform summarizes a shape by collecting diagrams from height sweeps in every direction. Each sweep tracks when features like holes appear and vanish, giving a rich fingerprint of the shape.

The transform is known to be continuous, stable, and able to tell apart broad classes of shapes. Kerber and Wang work on computing the bottleneck distance between two such transforms, the cost of matching one fingerprint to another. A workable distance lets software compare shapes in medicine, graphics, and data analysis.
arxiv-2512-00921:
Ahsan Javed and five coauthors review a key ingredient of materials modeling in a 2025 paper. Two-dimensional materials, sheets one or a few atoms thick, have reshaped nanoscience with properties unlike their bulk forms. As experiments race ahead, reliable computation is needed to sort which new materials are promising.

Exchange-correlation functionals are the part of density functional theory that captures how electrons interact, and the choice among them drives accuracy. The review covers their applications to 2D materials, the challenges they face, and their limits. A clear map of these tools helps modelers pick functionals wisely instead of by habit. The paper gives readers a plain guide to what each choice can and cannot do well.
arxiv-2512-01121:
Christine Awofeso, Patrick Greaves, Oded Lachish, and Felix Reidl design a practical algorithm for a graph measure in a 2025 paper. The 3-admissibility of a graph is a promising measure for spotting real-world networks with algorithmically favorable structure. Sparse, well-structured networks admit faster algorithms for many hard problems.

Their algorithm decides whether a graph's 3-admissibility is at most a given bound. They state its running time in terms of the number of edges and the bound, and its space in terms of vertices and the bound. A practical test lets analysts screen large real networks for the structure that makes them tractable.
arxiv-2512-01221:
A 2025 astronomy paper presents new radio observations of a supernova remnant in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The remnant, cataloged as N206, is nicknamed the Goat's Eye by the authors. It is the expanding wreckage of a star that exploded in our neighboring galaxy.

Observations at multiple radio frequencies map the remnant in fresh detail. Inside it sits a radio structure that is likely a pulsar wind nebula, a bubble blown by a spinning neutron star left behind. That inner structure has a striking zig-zag shape, which the authors analyze in detail. Multi-frequency maps help separate the shell's glow from the nebula inside.
arxiv-2601-22821:
Alex Elliott, Scott Parkins, and Takao Aoki propose a way to make linked light, steadily, from a single atom. The light sits in the telecom band, the range used by fiber networks. Two lasers, tuned with care, drive the atom up a two-photon path to a state that emits the wanted light.

A steady source of linked photons would fit well with existing fiber lines. It could serve quantum networks that send secure keys or link distant quantum machines. Single-atom sources are prized because they are clean, small, and well understood.
arxiv-2512-00121:
Johannes Hagel studies a nonlinear oscillator whose forcing changes in an irregular, non-repeating way, in a 2025 study. The system is a parametrically forced equation with a quadratic term. Hagel asks how such an oscillator behaves over long times.

The forcing term depends on a strictly positive solution of a weakly forced companion equation. The study examines the phenomenon named in its title, tube rupture, through theory and simulation together. Results of this kind matter for understanding driven mechanical and electrical systems that can drift into failure when forcing never settles into a pattern. Hagel's approach combines proof with numerical experiment, each checking the other. That pairing suits a system whose long-run behavior is hard to guess.
arxiv-2512-00421:
Epidemics unfold together with human beliefs and behavior, each shaping the other. Mulin Tian and Ajitesh Srivastava present TrendGNN in 2025, a graph neural network aimed at understanding epidemics, beliefs, and behaviors together. Most forecasting work predicts epidemic signals with simple mechanistic models or opaque deep models.

Black-box forecasters ingest every available signal without offering interpretability, so officials cannot see why a prediction moved. A graph-based model that links disease spread to behavior could show which social signals drive the forecast. That transparency matters when predictions guide school closures, vaccination drives, and hospital planning. Beliefs drive behavior, and behavior drives transmission, so the loop is the story. For health teams, the gain is a view of cause and effect. They can see which shifts in mood or habit push the curve up, and which pull it down.
arxiv-2512-00621:
AI music generators now compose whole songs, which threatens artistic authenticity and copyright alike. Arnesh Batra, Dev Sharma, and Krish Thukral present a method for detecting synthetic music in 2025, built on dual-stream contrastive learning. Existing detectors falter as new generators appear.

Earlier models such as SpecTTTra performed well at first, then dropped sharply on out-of-distribution content from newer systems. A dual-stream design compares two views of the audio to catch generator fingerprints that survive across systems. Reliable detection helps platforms label synthetic tracks and protects musicians whose styles are imitated. Contrastive learning teaches the detector by comparing streams rather than labeling songs. Detection must keep pace with generators that improve month by month.
arxiv-2512-03021:
Real data often mix a clear signal with messy noise. Ananyabrata Barua and Ayanendranath Basu wrote this 2025 study on how to find the true center of such data. Older tools, called mixture models, split mixed groups into smaller, cleaner parts.

The authors work on a flexible method that stays steady when noise is present. A steady center estimate matters when a few odd values could pull a result off course. Their approach fits fields like health, finance, and lab work, where mixed data are common. It gives analysts a safer way to name the main signal. Readers get a clear sense of why finding a center in messy data needs care.
arxiv-2512-02021:
Databases come in long-standing families: B-trees, log-structured stores, graph databases, and blob stores each handle one kind of job. Jun Kawasaki's 2025 paper proposes a ninth lineage, a functorial-categorical database called Enishi, built to fuse those jobs into one design.

Enishi separates watching the data, held in graph form, from the authority to persist it, handled categorically. It composes ownership, capability checks, content addressing, and graphs into a double categorical system. The stated goals are content that cannot change silently, capability-based safety, schema-free graph traversal, and coherence over time. It is a ground-up rethink of what a database is.
arxiv-2512-02221:
Two kinds of entropy share one formula and one name. One comes from heat and engines. The other comes from Shannon's theory of messages and code length. Dallin Fisher and Qi-Jun Hong show in 2025 that the two match in size for real solids and liquids.

They treat the atoms' layout as a source of messages. Then they gauge entropy from how well the paths of the atoms can be squeezed by data compression. No split of the system into parts is used, and no fitted model is used. A squeeze-based gauge could give a handy new way to get entropy out of computer models of matter.
arxiv-2512-02421:
Fine-tuning a vision-language model on one domain usually dulls its ability to handle new ones. Xinyao Li and five co-authors propose in 2025 dedicated prompt guidance as a way to adapt such models while protecting their domain generalization, the ability to work in unseen settings.

The usual recipe fine-tunes one universal model on the whole dataset, trading generality for fit. Guidance through dedicated prompts aims to steer the model per domain while leaving its broad skills intact. Keeping both sides of that trade-off matters for models deployed in the open world, where the next domain is never in the training set.
arxiv-2512-02521:
Laura Zarraoa and four co-authors chase one of the faintest signals in optics: a few photons hidden in sunlight. Counting such weak light demands filters that pass a narrow color band and block all else. Strong background light otherwise drowns the signal completely.

Earlier work showed that single trapped atoms can act as narrow band detectors with very low false counts. The team's atomic photodetector builds on that idea for signals buried in bright broadband light. Detectors of this kind could serve quantum communication and sensing tasks that must work outdoors in daylight. Daylight work has long been a blind spot for tests that chase the most faint light of all.
arxiv-2512-02621:
Panagiotis Papantonakis and four co-authors improve how captured scenes are textured in Gaussian splatting. Splatting has become a favorite way to rebuild real scenes in 3D and render them in real time. Fine surface detail, though, demands huge numbers of tiny primitives, which wastes memory.

Surfaces often mix smooth geometry with rich, busy appearance, or the reverse. Content aware texturing spends detail where the content needs it, not evenly everywhere. Leaner scenes render faster and store smaller, a gain for virtual reality, games, and digital copies of real places. The trick spends bits where the eye will look, and saves them where the eye will not rest.
plos-pone-0010021:
Rita Pinter and Robert Hindges studied mouse eye development in PLOS ONE in 2010, focusing on small RNA molecules called microRNAs. As eyes grow, nerve fibers from the retina must cross or turn at the optic chiasm, a key choice point. Getting that wiring right is what lets the brain build a proper picture from both eyes.

In mice lacking Dicer, an enzyme needed for microRNAs to work, the team found retinal defects. Fibers also went astray at the chiasm in these mutants. The findings show that fine-tuning by small RNAs is part of how the visual system wires itself.
plos-pone-0010221:
The authors were María Larriba, Juan Casado-Vela, Natalia Pendás-Franco, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study hunted protein targets of a cancer factor in human colon cancer. The factor, Snail1, drives a change called EMT, where cells loosen and gain invasive traits. Gene studies had listed many Snail1-regulated genes, several tied to tumor spread in different cell types.

Using proteomic analysis, a screen of proteins rather than genes, the team found novel target proteins. Protein-level evidence can catch changes that gene studies miss. Each new target adds to the map of how colon tumors become invasive.
plos-pone-0009821:
Graves' disease is an immune disorder that makes the thyroid gland overactive. Shuang-Xia Zhao and colleagues looked for gene links to the disease in China's Han population. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Han Chinese are the largest ethnic group in China.

The gene they examined is CTLA4, which helps set how active immune cells become. The study tested whether variants in that gene associate with Graves' disease. Immune genes are natural suspects in a disease where immunity attacks the thyroid. Findings in one population help show how widely the link holds.
plos-pone-0009921:
DNA microarrays read thousands of genes at once, but only if their probes are well chosen. Jennifer Mulle and colleagues put probe selection to an empirical test. Their evaluation appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Probes are short oligonucleotide strands fixed to the chip, each matched to one gene. Empirical evaluation means judging choices by real performance, not theory alone. Microarrays were the workhorse of gene studies for a decade. Bad probes blur results and can fake gene activity. The findings help labs design arrays that read genes cleanly. Chips can hold tens of thousands of probes.
